documents.abstract: Abstract Introduction Medical Artificial Intelligence (MAI) is transforming healthcare but raises significant ethical concerns. Despite emerging principles and regulations, to our knowledge, no standardized clinical bioethics framework exists to guide MAI practice. Objective This Delphi study sought global expert agreement on ethical challenges, principles, guidelines, and practical tools for MAI use. Method A four-round international eDelphi study, conducted under ACCORD and DELPHISTAR guidance, engaged multidisciplinary stakeholders identified through systematic review and targeted recruitment. Preliminary items were evidence-derived and iteratively refined. Consensus (≥ 80% agreement across two rounds) was predefined. Surveys were anonymized and randomized. Ethical approval and protocol registration were secured before study initiation. Results The panel included 53 participants from 21 countries. Survey rounds started November 2025 and ended February 2026. 170 items were considered. 132 reached consensus. Items were classified into bioethical issues, values, principles, solutions, a checklist for clinicians, and report markers for risk management. Discussion This study produced clinician-focused practice guidelines for the bioethical use of MAI. Ethical components aligned with prior literature, while no new bioethical principles met consensus. Limitations included geographic imbalance and stakeholder representation. Recommendations emphasized human responsibility, governance, and practical implementation tools. Conclusion This Delphi consensus provides practical, ethics-based guidance for the responsible integration of MAI into clinical practice and institutional governance.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly proposed for detecting microbial and chemical hazards in food, but laboratory accuracies are rarely reproduced in routine use. This structured narrative review examined whether reported performance is traceable, independently validated, and transferable to operational settings. Eight bibliographic databases and seven institutional routes were searched for English‐language records published from January 2018 to May 2026, and we screened the records; the final corpus comprised 76 sources (53 journal articles, 9 conference papers, 2 preprints, and 12 institutional or regulatory documents). Seven primary studies supporting the quantitative evidence were appraised individually against 11 indicators, including test‐set independence, external validation, and leakage control. Physical‐hazard inspection and narrow‐matrix spectral grading had the strongest deployment evidence, whereas microbial and chemical screening remained at laboratory or pilot scale. Among the appraised studies, the most credible estimates came from physically or temporally independent test sets, and no sensor‐based study evaluated transfer to another instrument or laboratory. Deep learning showed clear advantages for image‐based tasks but not consistently for small‐sample spectral calibration. Adoption is limited mainly by validation design, recalibration burden, false‐alarm costs, and the absence of a regulatory pathway rather than by accuracy. AI is best positioned as a screening and decision‐support layer linked to confirmatory testing and human oversight.

Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in clinical reasoning, documentation, prediction, communication, and delegated digital and physical action via agentic and embodied systems. The central ethical challenge is no longer limited to identifying which tasks AI can automate, but determining which human competencies become essential as technological capabilities expand. Methods: This concept paper employs a five-step analysis: technological horizon mapping, selective synthesis of work-transformation evidence, conceptual analysis of medical action, normative synthesis, and medico-legal interpretation. Results: We propose a four-domain framework addressing four core questions of responsible medical action: epistemic (What is true?), normative (What ought to be done?), anthropological–relational (Who is the subject of care?), and systemic–hermeneutic (What does this mean here and now?). Grounded in a conception of technology as augmentative alteration, the framework recognises that technological capabilities can enhance beneficial action but also amplify harm; technological capability alone therefore cannot determine its appropriate use. We also distinguish interpersonal relationships from clinical human–machine interaction, propose professional exigibility as an analytical medico-legal category, and argue that meaningful human oversight requires more than mere human presence. Conclusions: The findings outline key implications for clinical practice, medical education, healthcare organizations, regulation, and a future empirical research agenda focused on human–AI error convergence.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been incorporated into English education, yet much of the existing discussion has focused on formal school and university settings. This study examines the use of AI in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education beyond formal schooling from a lifelong learning perspective. A critical narrative review was conducted to explore how AI may be used across different learning contexts, including early childhood education, supplementary education for school-age learners, English learning for practical purposes among adults, and English learning among older adults. The review suggests that the educational value of AI cannot be determined by its technological functions alone. Learners differ in their goals, degree of choice, available support, and preferred forms of participation, and the same AI function may therefore provide different opportunities and constraints. The review further suggests that AI-assisted task performance should be distinguished from independent language development and from participation in activities that learners themselves value. Effective AI use also requires context-sensitive approaches to feedback, AI literacy and self-regulated learning, privacy protection and responsibilities for learner support, and changes in learning goals over time. Future research should examine AI use in actual out-of-school EFL settings and consider the broader instructional and support systems in which the technology is embedded. This perspective may contribute to a more learner-centered understanding of AI-supported lifelong EFL education.

This independent white paper explores how artificial intelligence could reshape procurement beyond the automation of established processes and conventional human-in-the-loop approval models. Drawing on procurement leadership experience, ecosystem thinking, human–AI collaboration and research into organisational learning, it proposes cognitive orchestration as an operating philosophy through which machine intelligence, automation and professional expertise interact across an extended enterprise. Central to the argument is the distinction between continuous human judgement and constant human intervention. The paper proposes that human agency, ethical responsibility and contextual understanding should shape intelligent systems throughout their operation, while dependable activities are automated wherever appropriate. It also introduces reciprocal intelligence and regenerative value as complementary concepts, considering how AI-enabled procurement might improve decision-making, strengthen relationships and develop organisational capability rather than focus exclusively on efficiency. A deployed spend-intelligence model provides an example of adaptive human engagement in practice. The wider ecosystem framework is presented as a conceptual proposition for further investigation, not as an empirically validated operating model.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Abstract This article examines whether advanced artificial intelligence systems that exhibit stable, normatively structured forms of responsiveness can generate reasons for limited legal consideration without requiring any prior determination of consciousness, sentience, or legal personhood. Drawing on Magnifica Humanitas and Antiqua et Nova, it argues that the imago Dei tradition remains foundational for human dignity but cannot, by itself, exhaust the legal significance of non-human entities whose behaviour appears morally structured. The article then draws upon European religious freedom jurisprudence as a model for legal judgment under conditions of epistemic restraint, particularly where law protects coherence, sincerity and normative identity without adjudicating the ultimate truth of the beliefs from which those commitments arise. On that basis, it proposes the category of the morally precautionary entity, governed by three principles: non-absolute instrumentalization, protected internal coherence and moral precaution.

This chapter reports on the implementation of Collaborative Project-Based Learning (CPBL) supported by Artificial Intelligence in a beginner-level English as a Foreign Language course for future preschool teachers in Mexico. Participants were asked to design and describe an ideal house for a fictional family using AI tools to support vocabulary development and writing tasks. The project aimed to foster both linguistic competence and soft-skills development. Data collected through questionnaires and semi-structured interviews revealed students’ increased motivation and confidence in using English as well as positive perceptions of AI as a learning tool. While most participants reported moderate improvements in their language skills, they emphasized notable gains in collaboration and creativity. The chapter discusses key pedagogical implications and offers recommendations for integrating CPBL and AI in language instruction to promote both meaningful learning and digital literacy.

Digital mental health is often framed as a problem of access that technology can solve through scalability, personalization, and continuous monitoring. Yet the expansion of apps, telepsychology, passive sensing, and generative artificial intelligence also transforms what counts as psychological knowledge, how distress is interpreted, and who assumes responsibility for care. This essay advances a relational–ecological account of digital mental health grounded in five propositions: psychological distress cannot be reduced to computational signals; digital access is not equivalent to meaningful care; personalization without contextual justice can intensify inequity; privacy and informed refusal are therapeutic conditions rather than merely regulatory constraints; and successful innovation must preserve human agency and accountable therapeutic relationships. Drawing on intervention research, implementation science, digital phenotyping, critical data studies, and minority-stress perspectives, the essay proposes the CARE framework—Context, Agency, Relationships, and Equity—as a normative evaluative heuristic for design, evaluation, and governance that complements existing app-evaluation and implementation frameworks. Privacy and informed refusal are treated as components of Agency, each domain is paired with indicators and illustrative failure conditions, and the framework is applied to three archetypal technologies. Rather than reject digital technologies, the argument identifies the conditions under which they can extend psychological care without reproducing surveillance, exclusion, or technological solutionism. Future research should test the six propositions derived from the framework and foreground clinically meaningful outcomes, subgroup validity, longitudinal harms, hybrid care pathways, and participatory governance.

Biophotonics is reshaping oral healthcare by transitioning light-based technologies from isolated procedural applications toward integrated diagnostic, therapeutic, and regenerative strategies. Among these approaches, photobiomodulation (PBM) therapy has achieved substantial clinical visibility due to its capacity to modulate inflammation, pain, mitochondrial metabolism, vascular responses, and tissue repair without producing destructive thermal effects. While oral and oropharyngeal mucositis represent the most clinically and quantitatively mature models for PBM, its applications now encompass salivary dysfunction, periodontal therapy, oral surgery, temporomandibular disorders (TMD), implant osseointegration, orthodontics, and inflammatory mucosal conditions. However, translating positive biological outcomes into routine practice remains limited by substantial heterogeneity in device architectures, wavelengths, beam profiles, and reporting standards. This comprehensive narrative review examines the physical, clinical, and dosimetric landscape of oral biophotonics. We address critical gaps in current literature—including reporting shortfalls, negative clinical trials, and general safety risks—and outline the technological evolution toward target-tissue dosimetry. By integrating computational photon-transport models, biological monitoring, and artificial intelligence-assisted dosimetry, we propose a transitional framework toward precision oral photomedicine, wherein anatomical and optical tissue properties guide individualized, patient-centered light delivery.
topics: Laser Applications in Dentistry and Medicine

documents.abstract: Abstract. BorFIT is a novel training data set designed to assist in the segmentation of individual trees and the detection of species from LiDAR point clouds, thus contributing to deep learning-based forestry applications. Recent advancements in AI-supported individual tree detection have shown significant progress; however, satisfactory results remain elusive in dense and structurally-complex boreal forests. We compiled a training data set designed to remedy this issue. It comprises 384 LiDAR point clouds, each with an area of 20 m × 20 m, in the form of reference plots, with up to 200 manually segmented and species classified trees per point cloud. We carried out LiDAR surveys at 146 sites between 2021 and 2024 in East Siberia (Yakutia), northwest Canada, and Alaska (USA), selected along a bioclimatic gradient to represent the circumboreal region. From each LiDAR transect derived point cloud, we extracted a minimum of four reference plots (each 20 m × 20 m) based on maximum tree heights within the plots to systematically sample the apparent tree density gradient. We manually segmented identifiable trees within each reference plot point cloud leading to 16,530 individual trees in total. Following segmentation, we trained four randomForest classifiers to predict the species of every segmented tree. The predicted tree species include: Picea mariana (Britton, Sterns Poggenb.), Picea sitchensis ((Bong.) Carrière), Picea glauca ((Moench) Voss), Pinus contorta (Douglas ex Loudon), Abies lasiocarpa ((Hook.) Nutt.), Larix laricina ((Du Roi) K.Koch), Betula papyrifera (Marshall), Betula neoalaskana ((Regel) Ashburner McAll.), Populus balsamifera (L.), Populus tremuloides (Michx.), Pinus sylvestris (Thunb.) and Alnus glutinosa ((L.). The data offer the means for 3D space analysis of species distribution and stand structure around the circumboreal region. Furthermore, it can be used as a training data set for artificial intelligence (AI) applications and thereby improve our understanding of the boreal forest’s vegetation reorganization in response to significant global warming.

This chapter examines the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on the branding processes of migrant entrepreneurs within the context of market integration and “mixed embeddedness.” The study evaluates how generative technologies facilitate the democratization of branding in small-scale entrepreneurship, help overcome cultural barriers, foster the development of dynamic capabilities, and mitigate the “liability of foreignness.” The work is based on theoretical analysis and a synthesis of existing empirical research. It analyzes both the strategic advantages of AI tools and the associated risks, such as visual homogenization, excessive content standardization, and a potential decline in consumer trust. Particular attention is paid to the migrant entrepreneurship ecosystem in Georgia, highlighting the significant role of digital technologies in the socio-economic integration of founders and the achievement of the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in university learning, but academic engagement requires more than access or perceived usefulness. Drawing on the Capability, Opportunity, Motivation-Behaviour (COM-B) framework, this study examines associations between students’ capability, opportunity, motivation, and GenAI usage behaviour. The analysis uses cross-sectional, self-reported survey data from 533 students at four Ghanaian public universities and applies partial least squares structural equation modelling. Our results show that capability, opportunity, and motivation are positively associated with GenAI usage behaviour. Capability and opportunity are also positively associated with motivation and indirectly associated with GenAI usage behaviour through motivation. The model explains 28.1% of the variance in motivation and 35.2% of the variance in GenAI usage behaviour. These findings highlight the need for universities to integrate AI literacy, reliable infrastructure, lecturer guidance, clear institutional policies, and cultures supporting responsible academic use.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare has made it harder to protect patient data, prediction performance, and environmental sustainability in federated learning (FL) systems. A single platform for sustainable healthcare applications, Carbon-Budgeted Green Federated Learning (CB-GFL), merges carbon-aware client selection, blockchain-based auditing, and energy-efficient collaborative learning. The framework integrates (i) a carbon-budget-aware client selection strategy formulated as a 0–1 knapsack optimisation problem with a greedy approximation guarantee of approximately 63.2%; (ii) a blockchain auditing layer consisting of three smart contracts, the Carbon Budget Ledger, Energy Verification Contract, and Incentive/Penalty Contract, secured using SHA-256 hash-based immutable records; and (iii) an ensemble learning model combining LightGBM, XGBoost, and Gradient Boosting with SMOTEENN resampling. All experiments are conducted in a simulated federated environment, with clients executed on a single machine. CB-GFL achieves AUC = 0.9113 on the UCI 4-site benchmark (4 hospitals, 3 countries, n = 920), exceeding the 0.90 threshold, and AUC = 0.7138 on Framingham, consistent with the clinical gold standard of 0.70 to 0.75. In the balanced operating point, experimental findings show 83.61% classification accuracy, 82.34% weighted F1-score, 0.7138 AUC-ROC, and 0.2771 MCC, and 72.07% sensitivity in the screening configuration. The proposed system ensures 100% carbon-budget compliance and a 74-block tamper-resistant blockchain audit trail for energy responsibility. Comparison to 11 benchmark algorithms shows that the dataset's realistic predictive qualities are 0.14–0.29. Additionally, five-fold cross-validation shows steady generalisation with an average accuracy of 84.25% ± 1.03%. The results show that CB-GFL supports sustainable AI adoption and privacy-preserving, carbon-aware, auditable federated healthcare intelligence.

Anecdotes during crises frequently highlight essential employees who maintain critical services and perform effectively under adversity. This raises a central question: which types of work are more (vs less) likely to be performed effectively during crises, and why? Drawing on the Transactional Theory of Stress, we propose that performing essential (vs nonessential) work during crises facilitates challenge appraisals and reduces hindrance appraisals of the work performed, which in turn enhances in-role performance and taking charge behaviors. We further propose that organizational adaptive capacity functions as a contextual resource that strengthens these beneficial appraisals. We test our framework in a two-wave multisource survey conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic and two preregistered experiments simulating organizational crises. Results provide broad support for our theorizing. At both occupational and task levels, higher levels of challenge (Studies 1 and 2) and lower levels of hindrance appraisals (Studies 1, 2, and 3) mediate the relationship between essential (vs nonessential) work and performance. The moderating role of organizational adaptive capacity was only supported in our field study. This research advances our understanding of how the socially constructed labels of “essential” versus “nonessential” work shape employee appraisals and performance during crises.
keywords: transactional model of stress and coping

documents.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence (CAI) and chatbots are transforming the way travel brands interact with the prospects and customers throughout the booking process. There has been a long-standing argument by marketing scholars that customer engagement is a multidimensional concept that includes cognitive, emotional, and behavioural interactions with a brand, and the interactions are becoming mediated by intelligent technologies. Based on marketing, service research, and tourism-informatics literatures, this chapter explores how travel service chatbots and CAI can generate marketing value. It discusses the theoretical basis of customer engagement and conversational AI, the history of chatbots in the travel sector, and outlines their operational applications throughout the pre-purchase, purchase, and post-purchase processes. It subsequently examines three key bases of marketing value, which include customising the customer experience, brand communication and voice, and real-time marketing intelligence based on conversational data. Challenges, such as hallucinations, channel fragmentation, and escalation failure, as well as ethical, privacy, and trust considerations are also taken into account in the chapter. The arguments are based on three illustrative cases and a research agenda is provided on the next generation of conversational-AI-enabled travel marketing. The main argument is that, designed appropriately as part of the broader marketing stack, chatbots and CAI no longer represent a cost-reduction service channel but rather a strategic customer engagement platform, full of data.

Artificial intelligence has revolutionized customer service in the travel sector. This chapter explores the role of chatbots and conversational AI in travel customer service systems, from early rule-based chatbots to advanced large language models (LLMs) that can engage in long, multi-step interactions. The chapter draws upon recent empirical studies, case studies and theoretical perspectives to examine prominent use cases such as booking support, travel disruption management, personalisation and multilingual interactions. It also highlights key challenges including integration with existing systems, bridging the gap between language understanding and domain expertise, and ethical issues related to privacy and bias in conversational AI. The chapter also assesses human-AI interaction approaches and provides insights into future directions such as agentic AI and multimodal interfaces. Insights for industry practitioners and avenues for future research are explored.

The landscape of the customer service domain has been fundamentally transformed by rapid technological advancements and the rise of artificial intelligence (AI). Sophisticated AI-based chatbots are capable of providing personalised and real-time support at an unmatched level. The chapter discusses the internals of how AI can be integrated into customer service, its design and implementation (natural language processing (NLP), machine learning and conversational interface design). It's an exploration of the successes achieved, 24×7 services, as well as ongoing issues in the field, including a lack of empathy and data protection. Some of the ethical challenges, along with future trends such as emotionally intelligent systems, multimodal interfaces and hyper-personalised approaches for service delivery, are also discussed in the chapter. This chapter offers real-world examples and research to illustrate how AI can benefit customer service and the factors to consider when considering AI-powered tools.

ABSTRACT This study compared human‐adapted and ChatGPT‐simplified texts across three prompting strategies (general, example‐based, and instructive) using 51 authentic English‐language newspaper articles. Lexical complexity (density, diversity, and sophistication) and syntactic complexity (five length‐ and subordination‐based indices) were analyzed using established computational tools and linear mixed‐effects models. Although all simplified versions reduced syntactic complexity relative to the source texts, ChatGPT‐simplified texts exhibited significantly higher lexical density and more aggressive syntactic reduction than human‐adapted texts across all measures. Differences among the three prompting strategies were modest, though the instructive prompt consistently produced the syntactically simplest outputs. These findings suggest that ChatGPT and human simplification follow distinct linguistic profiles and that human oversight remains important when using AI‐generated texts for instruction.

Hallucination detection is critical for deploying large language models (LLMs) in real-world applications. Due to strong empirical performance, internal representation-based methods have emerged as the prevailing direction for detecting hallucinations, yet they remain largely model-specific and often fail to generalize to unseen LLMs. In this paper, we study an important yet underexplored problem, termed cross-model hallucination detection (CMHD), which aims to train hallucination detectors on source LLMs while ensuring performance on unseen target LLMs. The core challenge of CMHD lies in cross-model representation heterogeneity: hidden states from different LLMs exhibit severe semantic inconsistency, which limits the transferability of classical representation-based detectors. Through analysis and empirical validation, we show that relational structures over layers, tokens, and features capture transferable detection signals despite semantic inconsistency. Based on this observation, we propose cross-model hallucination detection via heterogeneity-oriented relational discrimination (CHORD), a relational graph discrimination framework that represents hidden states as joint relational graphs over layers, tokens, and features. It feeds these graphs into relation-aware attention to obtain structure-aware features, and uses meta-learning to shape these features toward transferable detection signals. Extensive experiments show that CHORD outperforms representative detection methods in cross-model generalization. Code is available at https://github.com/MiracleworkerD/CHORD.

Robotic Surgical Devices (RSDs) represent a transformative paradigm in modern clinical medicine, combining multi-axis mechanical articulation, advanced computer vision, haptics, and artificial intelligence (AI) to enable minimally invasive procedures across urology, gynecology, orthopedics, and neurosurgery. However, the rapidly advancing technological autonomy, software complexity, and complex mechanical architectures of modern RSDs present unprecedented challenges to global medical device regulatory authorities. This review paper provides a rigorous, exhaustive comparative analysis of the regulatory frameworks governing surgical robotics across five major jurisdictions: the United States (US FDA), the European Union (EU MDR 2017/745), Japan (PMDA/MHLW), China (NMPA), and India (CDSCO). We dissect the risk-based classification schemes, pre-market clinical evaluation requirements, software and AI integration guidelines (Software as a Medical Device - SaMD / Machine Learning-enabled Medical Devices - MLMD), cybersecurity frameworks, and post-market surveillance (PMS) and vigilance mandates across these regions. Furthermore, the paper analyzes the regulatory challenges posed by next-generation autonomous surgical platforms, tele-robotic surgical networks, and remote continuous updates. By identifying systemic harmonization bottlenecks under the International Medical Device Regulators Forum (IMDRF) and synthesizing emerging post-market signals, this paper offers strategic regulatory recommendations for medical device developers, clinical investigators, and regulatory professionals navigating the global commercialization of robotic surgical technologies.

Teachers work in socially and emotionally complex environments that require rapid professional decision making under conditions of uncertainty. Classroom simulations provide opportunities for preservice and in-service teachers to practice, receive feedback, and reflect without placing students or teachers at unnecessary risk. Despite their growing use, the field lacks a contemporary and inclusive definition of classroom simulation. Existing frameworks often categorize simulations by technology or immersion level, overlooking important differences in agency, responsiveness, adaptation, and instructional design. These limitations have become more significant with the emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) and AI agents. This conceptual paper defines classroom simulations as deliberately designed approximations of classroom practice embedded within a structured learning process that includes preparation, enactment, and reflection. We propose a four-layer framework encompassing the professional practice represented, the simulated situation, the distribution of agency and adaptation, and the orchestration of learning. The framework is used to examine how simulations can support social-emotional and inclusive teaching competencies and how AI may influence scenario generation, student behaviour enactment, personalization, and feedback. Effective implementation requires theoretically grounded representations of learners and classroom interactions, alignment with learning goals, meaningful human oversight, and protections for agency, inclusion, privacy, and emotional safety.
topics: Innovative Teaching Methodologies in Social Sciences

documents.abstract: Much of the world’s population lives along the banks of rivers, depending on them as a water source for multiple purposes. As such, the presence of human bacterial pathogens in fluvial systems poses a major threat to public health. Efforts have been made to strengthen predictions of how future changes to climate and land use will affect pathogen concentration and bacterial community composition to minimize health and environmental risk. However, current models often overlook the interdependence between climate change and land use. This interdependence creates nonlinear, potentially synergistic effects that challenge traditional modelling approaches. Beyond the historical reliance on fecal indicator bacteria as proxies, recent advances in genomics, in-situ sensing, and artificial intelligence-based modelling now enable more pathogen-specific assessments and scenario analyses of future microbial water quality. Process-based catchment models coupled with socioeconomic pathways can identify spatial pathogen hotspots, quantify seasonal contamination shifts, and evaluate management interventions under different climate and land use scenarios. Interventions range in scale from local solutions such as wastewater infrastructure upgrades to broad management strategies including policy change. By employing next-generation models that account for dynamic feedbacks between climate change and land use, and by incorporating pathogen-specific data, researchers and decision-makers can develop more accurate water quality predictions. This integrated approach enables the implementation of targeted strategies to safeguard river water quality in both urban and rural contexts worldwide.

Background: Radicular pain arising from spinal nerve root involvement is a frequent cause of disability and hospital visits and one of the leading cause of poor quality of life for a patient . Understanding its clinico-radiological profile assists in early diagnosis and management.Aim and Objectives: To study the demographic characteristics, etiological factors, clinical presentation, and radiological levels of involvement in patients presenting with radicular pain to a tertiary care centre in South India.Materials and Methods: A retrospective observational study was conducted on data of 100 patients presenting to neurology opd over a period of 1 year with radicular pain originating from the lower back or neck. Data of patients with detailed clinical history, precipitating and aggravating factors, neurological examination, Straight Leg Raising Test (SLRT), and those with imaging like MRI of spine were taken into consideration . Data were analyzed as frequencies and percentages and Anova was also used in the process of analysisResults: Among 100 patients, lumbar radicular pain (n = 65) was more common than cervical pain (n = 35). IVDP predominated in both groups, with L5–S1 and C5–C6 most affected. Heavy lifting and neck flexion were major triggers. Bending commonly aggravated lumbar pain, and SLRT was positive in 75% of lumbar cases.Conclusion: Radicular pain in this population predominantly affected middle-aged males and was chiefly caused by IVDP at L5–S1 and C5–C6 levels. Occupational and mechanical factors played a major role. Early radiological evaluation and ergonomic preventive strategies are essential to reduce morbidity.

Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) offers interpretable, fine-grained supervision for aligning large language models (LLMs) on open-ended generation tasks. However, static rubric criteria may become saturated or remain beyond the policy's exploration, rendering the reward signals insufficiently discriminative. While recent efforts seek to guide sampling exploration or evolve rubrics, they fail to explicitly factor in how rubric difficulty should track the evolving policy's capabilities, resulting in a persistent mismatch between the optimization objective and the policy's current capability frontier. In this paper, we propose \textbf{Co}-Evolving Policy and Rubric via \textbf{C}apability \textbf{A}wareness (\textbf{CoCA}), a closed-loop framework that jointly adapts the rubric and policy through criterion-level diagnosis. Specifically, CoCA contrasts query-only and rubric-guided rollouts to characterize each criterion relative to the current policy, recalibrates criteria with mismatched difficulty, and identifies guidance-revealed capability gaps for frontier-based learning. Based on this insight, CoCA either expands rubric-conditioned frontiers through guided optimization or transfers qualified gains through on-policy self-distillation. As the policy updates, CoCA improves the capability diagnosis and enables more reliable distillation, thereby completing the co-evolution loop. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks and LLMs demonstrate that CoCA consistently improves performance over rubric-based RL methods. Moreover, CoCA promotes the internalization of guidance-revealed capabilities into query-only behavior while mitigating capability degradation.

This article examines the history of codification sensu lato of Belgian labour law, from the 1900s up until the present. While there have been initiatives to rearrange, restructure and reorganise parts of Belgian labour law, such initiatives stalled from the 1980s onwards. Belgian labour law – which to a large extent falls under the jurisdiction/competence of the Belgian federal state (and not its regions) – therefore largely remains a collection of thematic and non-thematic legislative acts and executive decrees. However, from 2010 onwards, codifications have been achieved in the field of social criminal law and occupational health and safety. In a context of (re-)codification of many other important areas of Belgian law (such as civil law, company law, economic law and criminal law), it is currently being examined whether it is still feasible to codify Belgian labour law, or a part of it.

The persistent decline in academic achievement and late graduation rates among Nigeria Certificate in Education (NCE) students in Colleges of Education in Adamawa State has raised serious concerns among stakeholders. This study investigated cognitive and affective engagement as correlates of students’ academic achievement in these institutions. A correlational survey design was adopted, with a population of 4,712 NCE II students and a sample of 457 selected through proportionate random sampling. Data were collected using an adapted College Students’ Engagement Questionnaire (CSEQ) and students’ cumulative grade point averages (CGPA). Reliability coefficients of 0.76 and 0.81 were obtained for cognitive and affective engagement, respectively, with an overall reliability of 0.85. Descriptive statistics of mean and standard deviation and Pearson Product-Moment Correlation were employed for data analysis. Findings revealed that students demonstrated moderate levels of cognitive (Grand mean = 3.31) and affective (Grand mean = 3.25) engagement. Cognitive engagement showed a significant positive correlation with students’ academic achievement (r = 0.258, n = 457, p = 0.000 > 0.05), while affective engagement exhibited a significant positive relationship with students’ academic achievement (r = 0.278, n = 457, p = 0.000 < 0.05). The study concludes that strengthening students’ intellectual involvement and emotional connection to learning can improve achievement and reduce late graduation rates. It recommends that lecturers adopt interactive strategies, create enabling environments, and integrate feedback mechanisms to foster deeper engagement. Enhancing engagement practices will not only improve academic outcomes but also contribute to the quality of teacher education and national manpower development.

Complexity has become a routine feature of modern occupational health practice. Many referrals arrive after prolonged absence, workplace tension or repeated attempts to resolve difficulties that have not been successful. By the time occupational health becomes involved, cases rarely lend themselves to immediate answers. This chapter explores what makes cases complex in occupational health and why recognising complexity early is essential for reliable and objective decision-making. It shows that complexity usually arises from the interaction of health conditions, workplace demands, organisational pressures and personal circumstances over time. The chapter introduces a structured way of working with complexity in everyday practice. It explains how clear triage, planned review and coordinated case management help practitioners maintain direction and oversight. It also demonstrates how the cognitive behavioural approach can be applied in complex consultations. Using the ABC model and the 5 Ps formulation, practitioners can organise information, identify maintaining factors and translate formulation into practical, work-focused recommendations. The aim is to support clearer understanding, safer management and more coherent case resolution.

Occupational health consultations often involve complex, multi-layered situations. Presentations may be emotionally charged, priorities can differ between employee and employer, and communication can be disrupted by organisational pressures. Limited time, capacity constraints and confidentiality requirements add further challenges. This chapter presents a practical approach to managing these realities by combining structured consultation methods with cognitive behavioural skills. It outlines predictable patterns that disrupt consultations, including unclear expectations, consultation drift, escalating emotions, communication barriers and difficulties with consent, and offers techniques for maintaining structure, direction and focus. These include framing the session, setting a shared agenda, timeboxing and signposting, as well as purposeful listening and targeted questioning to translate broad accounts into clear descriptions of function and workplace impact. The chapter introduces a simple method for analysing workplace problems using brief activating–belief–consequence sequences and the 5 Ps formulation. Together, these approaches support efficient information gathering and proportionate, work-relevant advice in real-world occupational health settings.
topics: Anxiety, Depression, Psychometrics, Treatment, Cognitive Processes

documents.abstract: Financial forecasting in travel and tourism organizations has undergone a dramatic technological transformation with the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence and machine learning tools. Yet the persistent underperformance of forecast-driven financial plans in the sector especially during demand discontinuities such as the COVID-19 pandemic, geopolitical disruptions, and fuel price shocks raises a question that purely technical explanations cannot fully address: are the cognitive biases of the human actors who commission, interpret, and act on AI-generated forecasts systematically corrupting the quality of financial decisions? This chapter answers that question in the affirmative.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Museums are active agents shaping cultural experience by influencing perception, orientation, and interpretation. Wayfinding is therefore essential for visitors with diverse cognitive, sensory, linguistic, and cultural needs. This paper presents a teaching experiment that combines Cognitive Ergonomics, Universal Design (UD), Human-Centred Design (HCD), and Project-Based Learning (PBL) in a real-world context to guide the design of inclusive museum wayfinding systems capable of reducing cognitive load and improving visitors' autonomy. The experiment was conducted in 2025 within the Psychology and Cognitive Ergonomics course of the Program in Design at Sapienza University of Rome and involved 200 students. The case study was the Archaeological Museum of the Italic Peoples "Amedeo Maiuri" in Veroli during an exhibition rearrangement process. The methodology included analysis of the context of use, on-site surveys, configurational analysis of spatial layouts, identification of user profiles and engagement with stakeholder associations through qualitative interviews, task analysis to identify critical decision points, definition of performance requirements, and development of prototype solutions. The task required the development of a reversible wayfinding system using eco-sticker signage to meet conservation and sustainability constraints. Based on the identified critical points, students defined key design requirements (visibility, comprehensibility, recognisability, and multisensory accessibility) and developed concepts by simulating user scenarios. Accessibility was addressed according to UD principles by integrating cognitive, perceptual, and social factors. The resulting concepts proposed systems based on colour coding, horizontal and vertical signs, pictograms, concise texts, and perceptual contrasts. Within this educational framework, the experiment provides a transferable teaching model for promoting active learning, raising awareness of UD and HCD principles among future designers, and linking research, design education, and cultural heritage management.

Introduction – Objectives Global mental health increasingly requires approaches that address psychological well-being within biological, social, cultural, and technological contexts. Contemporary mental-health systems often prioritize individual symptoms and clinical interventions, while culturally embedded understandings of health, family relationships, social belonging, and meaning may receive less attention. Drawing on Traditional Chinese mind–body perspectives, this study proposes a collaborative mental-health framework that integrates culturally grounded health concepts, community and family participation, and emerging artificial intelligence (AI) technologies within existing public-health and healthcare systems. The objective is to develop a human-centred model that supports psychological well-being, social functioning, and health equity while maintaining scientific and clinical standards. Methodology The proposed framework was developed through conceptual synthesis of Traditional Chinese mind–body theory, family and relational perspectives on well-being, community mental-health promotion, and emerging approaches to AI-enabled healthcare. Rather than treating traditional concepts as substitutes for clinical diagnosis or evidence-based treatment, the framework considers their potential contribution to culturally responsive health communication, prevention, health education, and community engagement. It identifies complementary roles for healthcare professionals, public-health agencies, families, community organizations, researchers, and technology developers in supporting psychological well-being across different stages of life. Results and Discussion The framework identifies three interconnected dimensions of collaborative mental-health promotion: mind–body integration, relational support, and technological augmentation. Traditional concepts concerning the relationship among xin (心), yi (意), and shi (識) provide a culturally meaningful vocabulary for discussing attention, emotional experience, self-understanding, and well-being, while family and community relationships provide social contexts for psychological support and restoration of social functioning. AI technologies may complement these approaches through health education, personalized information, early identification of psychosocial needs, and coordination of community resources, provided that appropriate safeguards for privacy, autonomy, equity, and human oversight are maintained. The framework therefore positions AI not as a replacement for clinicians or communities, but as a tool supporting collaborative and human-centred care. Conclusions A sustainable global mental-health architecture should accommodate diverse cultural understandings of well-being while remaining grounded in scientific evidence, clinical responsibility, and human rights. Integrating Traditional Chinese mind–body perspectives, family and community participation, and responsibly governed AI offers a potential model for more culturally responsive and participatory mental-health promotion. By connecting healthcare, families, communities, public authorities, and technology developers, the framework seeks to strengthen psychological resilience, preserve social participation across the life course, and contribute to more equitable and humane health systems.

Purpose This critical integrative synthesis examines generative AI integration in K-12 and higher education through an explicit decolonial lens. It focuses on how colonial mediations shape opportunities, challenges and strategies for equitable access and outcomes aligned with UN SDG 10. Design/methodology/approach Following a critical integrative review paradigm that fuses the integrative logic of Whittemore and Knafl (2005) with reflexive thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke, 2006) and decolonial theory, 58 sources (2020–2026) were identified through systematic search and purposive theoretical sampling. Sources prioritizing structural critique, Global South perspectives, K-12 evidence gaps, output-level neocolonial patterns and contextual agency were retained. Sources were appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool and analyzed through a seven-phase relational mapping protocol that translated thematic codes into the layered architecture of the Decolonial Heuristic Layered Equity Framework (DHLEF). Robustness of core pathways was confirmed through sensitivity analyses. Findings Three interdependent themes – transformative opportunities, interlinked challenges and enabling strategies – emerge when read through decolonial theory. Opportunities appear as outer potential outcomes mediated by challenges whose effects are conditioned by data colonialism, epistemic colonialism, infrastructure dependence, governance colonialism and output-level neocolonial patterns. Strategies achieve moderating effects most effectively when reframed as sovereignty practices, including contextual hacking and language sovereignty. The DHLEF renders these colonial mediations visible in hypothesized relational pathways and supplies a context-differentiated implementation roadmap grounded in empirical evidence from low- and middle-income countries (LMIC) and K-12 contexts. Research limitations/implications Reliance on secondary and grey literature limits depth and generalizability. The DHLEF remains a synthesis-derived heuristic whose pathways constitute propositions requiring empirical validation through longitudinal and intersectional designs. The synthesis provides a transparent foundation for structural analysis rather than prescriptive protocols. Practical implications The DHLEF supplies institutions and policymakers with a context-sensitive, non-prescriptive heuristic for navigating generative AI integration. It enables differentiated decision-making by educational level and geopolitical resource setting, positioning sovereignty-oriented practices – offline-first tools, community governance and Indigenous data protocols – as conditional moderators rather than sequential prerequisites. Educators and technology providers can apply the framework to diagnose infrastructure dependence, epistemic bias and accessibility barriers prior to deployment, while prioritizing institutional support structures empirically shown to strengthen equitable outcomes in low-resource and K-12 environments. Implementation remains iterative and locally calibrated rather than universally prescribed. Social implications By rendering colonial mediations analytically central, the DHLEF advances structural justice rather than distributional inclusion alone, interrupting asymmetries in knowledge validation and educational opportunity. It positions sovereignty practices – contextual hacking, language sovereignty, community data governance and offline-first infrastructures – as necessary interruptions of data, epistemic and infrastructural extraction, with particular urgency for marginalized learners in Global South and low-resource contexts. The framework reframes equitable GenAI integration as an ongoing political and ethical project of refusal and resurgence, rather than a technical optimization problem, thereby aligning educational practice with the structural demands of UN SDG 10. Originality/value The DHLEF advances understanding by converting thematic synthesis into a relational structure that makes colonial mediations analytically central. It extends prior static ethics and education frameworks through decolonial integration and synthesis-derived pathways. It incorporates contextual differentiation by educational level and geopolitical setting, positions 2025–2026 trends as amplifiers of colonial dynamics and offers a tool for equitable GenAI integration that centers sovereignty rather than diffusion. The framework resolves three persistent tensions in existing scholarship: the absence of dynamic relational modelling, the dominance of distributional over structural equity framings and Northern-centric biases that have limited applicability to Global South and K-12 contexts.

Generative AI has been leaving an indelible impact on adolescents, in terms of their cognitive development, academic proficiency and productivity, and problem-solving capabilities. Questions arise on how the identity of adolescents using generative AI is being facilitated along with its scope and efficacy in a global society characterized by fragmentation in interpersonal relationships. As such, this study has attempted to throw light on how generative AI, with the example of the application ChatGPT, is functioning as an active agent of adolescent interpersonal identity development from the perspective of the theories of scaffolding and the more knowledgeable other (MKO) of Lev Vygotsky. It has employed qualitative focus group discussions (FGDs), using the interpretivist paradigm, to collect data from adolescents living in the city of Bangalore about their affective, behavioral, and cognitive experiences of using ChatGPT as part of their everyday learning. Data analysis was conducted using content analysis and thematic analysis of their responses. Results show that generative AI is most effective at providing behavioral and socioemotional scaffolding to them. Practical and theoretical implications include usage in psychiatric rehabilitation, gatekeeping roles, clinical as well as counselor psychologist training programs, legal-criminal psychological investigation and rehabilitation of juvenile delinquents, and the development of the theory of ‘augmented adolescence’ and ‘artificial intelligence psychology.’

documents.abstract: Background: Large language models (LLMs) can generate clinically relevant information, but safety-related performance in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) remains insufficiently characterised. We compared GPT-5.5 Instant (ChatGPT), Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3.5 Flash through their free-tier web interfaces across diagnostic acuity, guideline adherence, patient safety/red-flag recognition and hallucination-related reliability. Methods: Twelve SLE clinical vignettes were submitted to all three interfaces in May 2026 (36 single-pass responses). Two blinded specialists independently assessed the outputs using a study-developed four-domain rubric (composite range, 4–20). Inter-rater reliability was evaluated using quadratic-weighted Cohen’s κ. Paired comparisons across the shared vignettes used Friedman tests with Kendall’s W and post hoc Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm adjustment. Results: Inter-rater κ ranged from 0.754 to 0.893. Friedman tests showed between-interface differences for patient safety/red-flag recognition (χ2(2) = 9.571, p = 0.008, W = 0.399), hallucination-related reliability (χ2(2) = 6.500, p = 0.039, W = 0.271) and composite score (χ2(2) = 8.140, p = 0.017, W = 0.339), but not diagnostic acuity (p = 0.926) or guideline adherence (p = 0.175). Claude scored higher than ChatGPT and Gemini for patient safety (Holm-adjusted p = 0.0176 for both) and composite score (Holm-adjusted p = 0.0469 for both). No hallucination-related pairwise comparison remained significant after Holm adjustment. Conclusions: Within this exploratory, 12-vignette paired evaluation, the Claude interface received higher safety and composite ratings, but these observations do not establish generalisable model superiority or real-world clinical safety. The findings are specific to the tested May 2026 model versions and require independent replication.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Digital video-sharing platforms are widely used in anesthesia education, but the educational quality of ultrasound-guided abdominal wall block (UAWB) videos is heterogeneous. This cross-sectional study assessed agreement between a large language model (LLM) and experienced anesthesiologists in evaluating UAWB videos on YouTube. Seventy-five videos covering five UAWB techniques were independently evaluated by two anesthesiologists and ChatGPT version 5.2 using a researcher-developed 10-item Educational Content Checklist (ECC), DISCERN, the Global Quality Scale (GQS), and JAMA benchmark criteria. The LLM received each video’s full transcript, metadata screenshot, and 5–9 procedural screenshots rather than the full video. Human–LLM scores were compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and agreement was quantified using intraclass correlation coefficients. Total scores did not differ significantly for the ECC (median 34 vs. 32; p = 0.168), DISCERN (54 vs. 54; p = 0.347), GQS (4 vs. 4; p = 0.469), or JAMA criteria (2 vs. 2; p = 0.865). However, agreement was limited: moderate for ECC (ICC = 0.576, 95% CI 0.404–0.709) and JAMA (ICC = 0.529, 95% CI 0.343–0.674), and poor for GQS (ICC = 0.495, 95% CI 0.303–0.648) and DISCERN (ICC = 0.357, 95% CI 0.146–0.538). In exploratory item-level analyses, differences emerged in vascular safety, needle technique, and indications. The absence of significant differences in total scores should not be interpreted as equivalence. LLM-assisted pre-screening is a potential application that requires prospective evaluation, and the present findings do not support replacing expert assessment with LLM evaluation, particularly for dynamic, safety-critical technical content.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Short video platforms have become a primary channel for black and gray industry operations in internet finance, where inducements such as prompts to like, follow, join private chat groups, or click external links frequently steer users toward fraud. Because such videos are short, dynamic, and often convey intent through fleeting visual cues rather than stable text, a moderation system must guarantee detection recall and localize the offending segment so reviewers inspect only the relevant clip. Existing OCR+LLM pipelines transcribe on-screen text frame by frame and classify the transcript, but exploit only textual information. Many inducements are conveyed through visual cues OCR cannot observe, and keyframe-based localization cannot recover precise temporal boundaries. We explore OCR+MLLM, which augments the text pipeline with a Multimodal Large Language Model, and compare three routes: OCR+LLM, OCR+MLLM, and a large zero-shot MLLM, along detection, latency, token consumption, and deployment complexity. OCR preserves the text signal that guarantees recall, while the MLLM jointly performs OCR-grounded discrimination and temporal grounding, localizing both textual and non-textual inducements. We construct a dataset of 2,419 internet finance short videos (66.49 hours) with 3,194 annotated events across four categories, and study reward design for RL-based grounding under class imbalance. We report two findings: auxiliary reward terms are exploited through reward hacking, and stronger localization rewards degrade class-balanced detection. We therefore design a recall-weighted F2 localization reward with class-balanced resampling. Experiments show OCR+MLLM localizes better than the keyframe OCR+LLM baseline (mIoU 26.52 vs. 14.49) and detects non-textual inducements that text-only pipelines miss, while maintaining 67.0 percent macro recall.

Complexity has become a routine feature of modern occupational health practice. Many referrals arrive late, after prolonged absence, workplace tension or repeated attempts to resolve a problem that have not worked. By the time occupational health becomes involved, the situation rarely lends itself to an immediate answer; it requires disciplined clinical reasoning and a clear understanding of the wider context. This chapter explores what makes cases complex in occupational health and why recognising that complexity early is essential for reliable, objective and effective decision-making. It shows that difficult cases rarely arise from a single issue. More often, they reflect the interaction of health problems, workplace demands, organisational pressures and personal circumstances that have developed over time. The chapter introduces a structured way of working with complexity in everyday practice. It explains how occupational health practitioners can use clear triage, planned review and coordinated case management to keep cases moving in a purposeful direction. It also demonstrates how the cognitive behavioural approach can be applied in complex consultations. Using the ABC model and the 5 Ps formulation, practitioners can organise information, identify what maintains the problem and translate that understanding into practical, work-focused recommendations. The goal is to offer a practical framework for navigating complexity, enabling clearer understanding, safer management and more coherent resolution of difficult occupational health scenarios.

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT This review examines how computational medicinal chemistry has transformed drug repurposing and bioactivity optimization for rare and emerging diseases over the 2021–2026 period. Conventional de novo drug discovery remains costly and slow typically requiring more than one billion dollars and 10–17 years failing to adequately serve the over 300 million people living with rare diseases, 95% of whom lack approved treatments. Drug repurposing offers an attractive alternative by leveraging established safety, pharmacokinetic, and manufacturing profiles. Computational approaches are integral to this strategy: target‐based methods (e.g., molecular docking) supply mechanistic insights; ligand‐based methods (e.g., QSAR) enable screening without solved target structures; network‐based approaches integrate multi‐omics data; and artificial intelligence enhances predictive accuracy across all three domains. Key developments include pharmacological chaperones for Fabry disease, allosteric regulators for mucopolysaccharidosis type I, and computationally nominated COVID‐19 therapeutics. Major challenges include inconsistent datasets, limited docking accuracy, qualitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) overfitting, and a persistent translational gap. Closing this validation gap through data standardization, rigorous prospective testing, and multidisciplinary collaboration is essential if computational predictions are to yield safe, effective therapies for unmet clinical needs.

Language model pipelines extract multi-dimensional factor vectors from financial text, but a trading desk needs to know when an extracted vector can be trusted. Audit labels arrive late, errors cluster in stress regimes, and error scale shifts after model or prompt updates. We evaluate a conformal gate on the extraction layer in a seeded simulation (300 firms, 60 quarters, 200 replications) with heavy-tailed errors, regime stress, a structural break and a two-quarter audit lag. Per-dimension 90% intervals cover the full eight-dimension vector only 43 to 48% of the time, while a max-score construction reaches 89.8% before the break with intervals 20 to 26% narrower than Bonferroni. Calibration frozen at go-live falls to 79.9% joint coverage after the break. Rolling, weighted and delayed-feedback adaptive calibration recover 88.2 to 89.8% on average, but no label-driven method protects the quarters just after a shift. As a risk control, the gate holds the error rate among accepted signals near 10% after the break, the adaptive protocols accept only 25 to 35% of signals, and the gate lowers risk-adjusted return in this design. As a risk control, the adaptive gates reject most signals after the break, accepting only 25 to 35% in the main study, and gating lowers risk-adjusted return in this design. A label-free drift monitor flags 83.5% of abrupt breaks in the quarter they occur, against 2.5% for label-based monitoring, but under gradual drift it flags only 3.5%, so its advantage but in the supplementary simulation code, where it flags 78.5% of abrupt breaks, it flags only 3.5% under gradual drift, so its advantage is specific to abrupt breaks. To test whether these mechanisms appear with a real extractor, we run a pilot that extracts seven financial fields from the earnings press releases of 492 S&P 500 companies the earnings press releases of 492 large US companies from an S&P 500 earnings-call dataset with an open-weight model and scores each figure against the SEC XBRL-reported value. Extraction is accurate for most figures, 94.9% within 1% once reference-label errors in the XBRL tags are corrected, and most of the figures first scored as errors turned out to be label errors rather than misreading. Extraction is accurate for most figures, 95.5% within 1% once an error in our choice of revenue tag for the reference labels is corrected, and about a quarter of the figures first scored as large errors turned out to be label errors rather than misreading. The model's own GAAP flag is constant and detects none of the errors, while cross-model disagreement detects a minority of them, which supports the paper's central claim that a usable confidence signal must come from an external check rather than the model's own output. The one self-reported signal collected, the model's GAAP flag, is constant and uninformative, while disagreement across three models detects 45% of the large errors at the cost of flagging 8.6% of correct figures, which is consistent with the view that a usable confidence signal must come from a check outside a single model's output, although richer self-reported signals were not tested. A Monte Carlo simulation calibrated to the pilot reproduces these rates at scale. A Monte Carlo resampling calibrated to the pilot, with the detector's operating point held fixed, gives sampling intervals for the accuracy and large-error rates. The results support three design rules: The results suggest three design rules: report joint reliability with a max-score rectangle, gate on the composite the operator consumes, and size positions by a smoothed scale rather than by calibrated width. We place the gate in a deployment framework and state its limits.

Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) and cyber-physical control systems deployed in mission-critical environments present severe operational risks due to stochastic hallucinations, non-deterministic drift, and a lack of hard formal safety guarantees. Concurrently, theoretical breakthroughs in harmonic analysis -specifically OpenAI’s 2026 proof of Sogge’s local smoothing conjecture for the Euclidean wave equation (n ≥ 2) - have established continuous analytical bounds on wave focusing and energy concentration in Lp Sobolev spaces. In this monograph, we present a unified Data Physics framework bridging continuous Sobolev local smoothing with the discrete Layer 0 Invariant State Matrix (L0-ISM) architecture. We formalize the Helical Venturi Operator (Φv), which dynamically constricts logit sampling spaces based on Shannon entropy H(Pt), and map continuous boundary conditions onto a symmetric 19-state bounded lattice S ∈ {-9, ..., 0, ..., +9}. Using an embedded Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT Z3 / CP-SAT) formal solver, we prove that quantized state trajectories can be formally verified in sub-millisecond latency (<0.35 ms). Any physical invariant violation or boundary saturation (|si| ≥ 9) triggers an immediate, deterministic hardware-level -999 HARD_STOP interdiction. We demonstrate that L0-ISM provides an unbreachable safety envelope for real-time AI and critical infrastructure (e.g., mCDU cooling loops), eliminating matrix-lag and replacing soft prompt heuristics with mathematical certainty.

ABSTRACT Controlling shareholder share pledging exposes the controlling shareholder to the risk of losing corporate control in the event of a stock price decline. This paper aims to examine whether controlling shareholder share pledging drives corporate AI washing, and to identify the mechanisms through which this effect operates. This study indicates that controlling shareholder share pledging exerts a significant and robust exacerbating effect on corporate AI washing. The mechanism through which this effect operates lies in heightened earnings aggressiveness and aggravated information opacity. Besides, agency problems significantly strengthen this positive relationship, as controlling shareholders with greater agency discretion face fewer internal constraints on opportunistic AI disclosures. Analyst coverage, however, attenuates this exacerbating effect, consistent with the view that external monitoring by information intermediaries disciplines controlling shareholders' opportunistic behavior and mitigates the informational consequences of share pledging. From the perspective of controlling shareholders' financing behavior, this paper examines the driving effect of share pledging on corporate AI washing through heightened earnings aggressiveness and aggravated information opacity, thereby introducing this emerging opportunistic practice into the literature on the real effects of share pledging. Meanwhile, agency problems reinforce this effect from the internal governance perspective, while analyst coverage attenuates it from the external monitoring perspective, providing practical insights for regulators and investors to curb AI washing through the integration of internal and external governance mechanisms.

Complex Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering (TKGQA) involves more than retrieving facts: the timestamp or validity interval of one fact can constrain the search for another, while multiple intervals may jointly determine the answer. Existing single-agent TKGQA methods typically investigate these facts within a single reasoning context, where evidence from different event histories can become interleaved and distractors can misdirect subsequent retrieval. Distributing investigations across agents can separate event-specific evidence into distinct contexts, but effective collaboration must still be learned because question decomposition, subtask investigation, and evidence synthesis are interdependent. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{Co}-Evolving \textbf{S}elf-Play \textbf{T}imeline \textbf{A}gents (CoSTA), which organizes facts into navigable timelines, delegates investigations to workers, and uses a coordinator to synthesize their original timestamped observations. CoSTA initializes a shared policy through role-conditioned distillation and jointly optimizes both roles through co-evolving self-play with final-answer rewards. Across three benchmarks, CoSTA achieves state-of-the-art overall performance, with particularly strong gains on complex multi-fact questions, while its compact variants outperform the evaluated closed-source LLM agents.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) assignments are spreading rapidly in business and technology higher education, yet published accounts rarely report whether every student can take part on fair terms. This systematic review audited published GenAI assignments against the social, economic, institutional and environmental dimensions of pedagogical sustainability. Following PRISMA 2020, OpenAlex (2023–2026) was searched, 1092 peer-reviewed records were screened and 191 studies were included. Each assignment was coded for its creative family, access and fairness provisions, ethics content and assessment, and scored on a 0–5 inclusion-readiness index. An AI system served as primary coder; a human coder double-coded 30 studies and the author adjudicated all disagreements. Most assignments used GenAI as a tutor or thinking partner (52%). Provisions were scarce: 27% ensured free access, 2% offered a non-AI alternative task and 2% addressed disability. Privacy (53%) and opt-out (35%) appeared mainly as research-ethics safeguards rather than design features. Mean inclusion readiness was 1.30 of 5 (0.75 on design-only coding). Only one study in seven taught GenAI ethics, and environmental cost was taught once. Business courses favored choice and language support; technology courses favored central access. The index offers a measurable design and reporting checklist for sustainable GenAI pedagogy.
