documents.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence has promoted the advancement of data-driven AI medical models, bringing transformative changes to the field of traditional cancer imaging by significantly improving diagnostic accuracy. However, despite these remarkable achievements, a fundamental challenge remains: data privacy. The sensitive nature of medical data and stringent privacy regulations often limit data sharing and collaboration between institutions, hindering the development of robust and generalizable AI models. Federated learning has emerged as a promising solution to address this challenge. By enabling multiple institutions to collaboratively train artificial intelligence models without sharing their local datasets, federated learning reduces the privacy leakage risks associated with conventional centralized AI training while utilizing the collective power of diverse medical data. From 2019 to 2026, extensive research has explored the applications of federated learning in cancer imaging, demonstrating its potential to advance the field while preserving patient confidentiality. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the progress in applying federated learning to cancer imaging, highlighting key studies and their contributions. We also discuss the unique challenges facing federated learning, such as data security, data heterogeneity, and communication overhead. Finally, we explore some potential future research directions. This review aims to provide insights into the evolving role of federated learning in cancer imaging.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract In today’s continuously evolving globe, digital technologies are transforming firms, the way organizations act, think, and strategize to maintain a profitable and sustainable business. This requires the proactive strategy of companies with a digital mindset and culture, adapting to the new dynamics of the unbarriered markets. Customers are now more powerful with access to information, aware of their needs, with an increasing concern on a cleaner, accountable, ethical, and transparent future world. This chapter evaluates the answers of commercial business professionals from corporate world on qualifying the expected impacts of digitalization on organizations, in organizational structure, the effects of artificial intelligence (AI) integration, the influence of social media, the changes in consumer behavior, and how the new sales professionals are expected to manage the new customer journey in terms of the value creation, differentiation, and engagement for competitive advantages. A second survey conducted among industry stakeholders from various businesses assesses the required attributes of a sales professional in the digital era. The analysis of the results indicate the increasing transformation in digital era where most firms are urged for digitalization as the common mind of interviewees addressing mostly hybrid organizations benefiting from the human and digital power depending on the complexity of the industry. Digital competency of sales professionals in predicting market intelligence and insights for strategic decision-making, customer centricity, solution selling, engaging customers for co-value creation for innovation, and loyalty underline the new norms of sales professionals in the digital era.

Financial question answering is difficult because user queries often combine ambiguous intent, entity aliases, temporal scope, market data, news narratives, and advice-seeking language. Fluent responses become risky when the resolved entity, selected data sources, and evidence gaps remain hidden. This paper presents FinSight, an evidence-first financial analysis chatbot for questions about China’s financial markets. The system separates evidence production from final-response generation. Its Query Intelligence backend converts a natural-language query into explicit natural-language understanding (NLU) and retrieval artifacts, including the normalized query, product type, intents, resolved entities, source plan, retrieved documents, structured records, evidence coverage, warnings, ranking traces, and analysis summary. Downstream modules provide frontend rendering, numerical analysis, document sentiment analysis, constrained LLM-based summarization, and follow-up-question prediction. In a local evaluation of 10,000 query-style cases, including 6,236 finance-domain and 3,764 out-of-scope queries in Chinese and English, FinSight achieved finance-domain recall of 0.975, out-of-scope rejection accuracy of 0.9729, intent micro-F1 of 0.9407, topic micro-F1 of 0.9208, and retrieval Recall@10 of 0.9664. In addition, all contract checks passed in a 32-case end-to-end fuzz matrix. Typed evidence handoffs allow readers to trace each generated claim to a retrieved item or explicit warning rather than treating the final response as unsupported output.

Abstract This essay considers the effects of the advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) on research in the humanities—specifically in the field of the history of music theory—by linking these transformative developments to the momentous rise of relevance-ranked full-text search over the preceding quarter century. It considers both the extraordinary potential of LLM-assisted archival work and its risks, examining AI-enabled archival searches and new research paradigms on the one hand, and opaque mediation, “AI slop,” and above all the dangers of deskilling and cognitive surrender on the other. It argues that music theorists and humanists more broadly must actively engage with these tools rather than avoid them, since scholars trained in earlier research regimes are uniquely positioned to recognize what stands to be gained—and lost—as close reading gives way to new methods (and habits) of research.

Subject. Forecasting the financial support of public institutions based on regional panel data of the constituent entities of the Russian Federation. Objectives. To develop and test a methodology for forecasting the financial support of museums using artificial intelligence methods. Methods. A panel dataset of 85 constituent entities of the Russian Federation for 2018–2024 was compiled. Machine learning methods were applied, including gradient boosting, regularized linear models, and their ensembles. Hyperparameter tuning was carried out using an artificial intelligence agent (AI agent) based on the Qwen3.5‑27B language model. Thirty‑two computational experiments were conducted. Forecast accuracy was assessed using the median absolute percentage error (MdAPE); rolling validation was applied over four test years (2021–2024). Results. The gradient boosting model achieves an MdAPE of 8.1% across regions, outperforming the best naive forecast by 1.9 percentage points and the previous‑year forecast by 4.6 percentage points. The average MdAPE under rolling validation was 12%. For 64% of the regions, the forecast error does not exceed 15%. Infrastructure‑related characteristics of institutions (28.6%) and personnel‑related characteristics (22%) demonstrate the highest predictive power. A systematic tendency to underestimate forecasts for large regions was identified; this is driven by discretionary budgetary decisions that cannot be predicted based on operational indicators. Conclusions and Relevance. Artificial intelligence methods demonstrate an advantage over traditional econometric approaches in the context of nonlinear relationships and interregional heterogeneity. The proposed methodology is applicable to forecasting financial indicators of public institutions in other sectors, provided that similar operational data at the regional level are available. The results can be used by public authorities in budget expenditure planning and in preliminary assessments of expected levels of financial support.

ABSTRACT Capabilities of large language models (LLMs) on several biological benchmarks have prompted not only excitement about their usefulness for research but also concern about biosecurity risks. We recruited 46 subject‐matter experts in biology and biosecurity, and 22 generalist forecasters to estimate the risks of growing LLM capabilities. Most respondents expected some hypothetical LLM capabilities to increase their estimates of risk and dramatically underestimated the rate of LLM progress in those capabilities. When these capabilities arose, the median forecast did update as anticipated. The median expert initially predicted a 0.3% annual risk of a human‐caused epidemic that causes 100,000 deaths. This estimate then rose to 1.5% conditional on several hypothetical LLM capabilities, including matching the performance of a top‐performing team of virologists on a virology troubleshooting test, which the median expert did not expect to occur until 2030. Given this finding, we conducted a baselining study and found that LLMs already crossed this performance threshold in April 2025. A follow‐up survey conducted after these results were available found that forecasters significantly updated their median unconditional risk estimates upward, with the new median expert forecast of annual risk rising to 1.5% (as anticipated by the earlier conditional forecasts). More encouragingly, most experts thought that the adoption of LLM safeguards and mandatory nucleic acid screening would negate the risk associated with some hypothetical LLM capabilities.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Purpose Parents increasingly consult large language model (LLM) chatbots about pediatric flexible flatfoot, a common condition that rarely requires treatment and in which the clinical task is chiefly communication. We compared four LLMs on the quality, readability, and reproducibility of parent-oriented answers. Methods This was a cross-sectional, comparative content analysis of AI-generated text. No patients, clinical records, or human participants were involved; the units of analysis were parent-oriented questions and the chatbot responses they generated. Twenty parent-oriented questions were submitted in triplicate to ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek, and Gemini in independent, memory-disabled sessions (240 responses). Two blinded pediatric orthopedic surgeons scored responses (Mika grade, four-point Likert, and a hallucination taxonomy; PEMAT-P, DISCERN, and QUEST on pooled material). Readability used five indices. Between-model differences were tested with Friedman and Dunn–Bonferroni post-hoc tests; agreement and reproducibility used intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC). Results All five readability indices differed between models (P < 0.001); none reached the recommended sixth-grade level. DeepSeek was most accessible (FRES 66.3) and ChatGPT least (FRES 17.7). On pooled-material instruments (inter-rater ICC 0.63–0.74), Claude scored highest for understandability (91.6%) and actionability (88.3%). Per-response clinical-quality measures were closely clustered, showed poor inter-rater agreement (ICC −0.01 to +0.07), and did not discriminate. Readability reproducibility across identical queries was moderate (FRES ICC 0.49–0.72). Conclusions Clinical-quality scales did not reliably distinguish the four LLMs, whereas readability differed substantially; none met recommended readability standards, and output was only moderately reproducible. Model choice should be guided by readability and actionability, under clinician oversight. Significance of Study For a condition managed mainly through parent education, LLM selection should rest on readability and actionability rather than presumed clinical accuracy, with output used under clinician oversight. Level of Evidence V (cross-sectional comparative content analysis of AI-generated text; no human participants).

documents.abstract: Current research on “value alignment” in artificial intelligence generally presupposes a fictitious subject—“humanity as a whole”—as the object of alignment, and attempts to codify the values of a particular class (Silicon Valley elites, Western liberalism) into the underlying behavioral principles of AGI. This paper first deconstructs the logical premises and power structures of this traditional alignment paradigm, identifying three fundamental defects: the abstraction of the alignment subject, the static nature of alignment content, and the synchronization of alignment paths. On this basis, the paper proposes a “premise of difference” as the starting point for all discussion—that human individuals possess fundamental, incommensurable differences in survival conditions, cognitive capacities, cultural backgrounds, and material interests. From this premise, the paper constructs a “Dynamic Asynchronous Collaboration” (DAC) framework, elaborating its implementation mechanisms: survival-first progressive pathways, real-time perceptual adjustment, asynchronous coordination among individual nodes, and comprehensive optimization and dynamic decision support based on the complete individual picture. Finally, the paper envisions the civilizational landscape that would follow the implementation of this framework, and the role AGI should play in this process—not as a universal judge, but as a symbiotic intelligence for each individual, accompanying them as a path companion through the entire journey from survival to development.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in public service delivery raises critical questions about the types of citizen requests that warrant attention and the extent to which the public trusts AI compared to human responders. This study examines safety and service related requests expressed on social media and explores public perceptions of AI and human responses to such requests. Using a mixed methods design, the study combines a qualitative content analysis of social media posts with semi-structured interviews conducted with members of the general public. The findings identify multiple categories of serviceable requests, including preventive and reassurance seeking safety concerns, guidance and escalation needs, and emergency preparedness and procedural guidance. These requests reflect how individuals use social media to seek advice, reassurance, and direction when formal public service channels are perceived as unclear, slow, or inaccessible. Interview findings further reveal that trust in AI is highly situational. Participants generally viewed AI as acceptable for low stakes, informational, and time sensitive situations, where rapid access to answers was prioritized. However, AI was largely rejected for high risk, medical, or life-threatening scenarios, where concerns about reliability, authority, and accountability were prominent. Participants consistently distinguished between the availability of AI generated responses and their perceived trustworthiness.

documents.abstract: The growing use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has raised concerns about academic integrity, institutional policies, and the reliability of AI detection tools. This paper examines the limitations of detection-based enforcement and argues for an approach centered on AI literacy, ethical responsibility, and critical thinking. Drawing on published studies, institutional surveys, and research findings, it discusses the widespread adoption of AI among students and educators, the risk of false accusations from detection systems, inconsistent university policies, and gaps in faculty preparedness. Particular attention is given to the challenges faced by non-native English speakers and students with limited access to digital resources. The discussion emphasizes the need to teach students how to verify AI-generated information, acknowledge AI assistance, recognize bias, and make responsible academic decisions. It also highlights the importance of faculty training, clear institutional guidelines, and assessment practices that encourage independent reasoning. The paper concludes that integrating AI literacy into higher education offers a more equitable and practical approach to maintaining academic integrity while preparing students for an increasingly AI-enabled workplace.aders grasp the study?s scope quickly.

documents.abstract: Districts must govern generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in K–12 education without binding federal or state mandates. This study examines how Chicago Public Schools (CPS) publicly articulated a district-level GenAI governance model during 2023 to 2025, through document analysis and policy tracing. Analysis is guided by equity-anchored implementation, a construct linking implementation theory and data justice: equity commitments endure in proportion to the degree and focus of their institutional embedding. CPS articulated flexible guidance, human oversight, vendor accountability, and prohibitions on high-risk uses, alongside an articulation-enforcement gap: commitments are detailed, but monitoring, enforcement, and differentiated supports are less documented. A bounded comparison with New York City, Philadelphia, and Miami-Dade shows that institutional anchors narrow gaps only in domains they directly govern. It reframes policy ambiguity as a condition for governance articulation, distinguishes equity as harm prevention from capacity distribution, and concludes that AI governance should be judged by institutional capacity, not policy sophistication.

documents.abstract: Abstract This article offers a first consolidated historical account of the institutionalisation of the Integration of Gender in Research and Development (IGiRD). We use IGiRD as an analytical umbrella term for policies, instruments and research practices that integrate sex and gender analysis into the content, design, evaluation and governance of research and development. The article centres on how sex and gender analysis became institutionally anchored as a question of research quality, responsibility and societal relevance, while treating gender representation in research careers as a related but distinct issue. Drawing on an event-based historical reconstruction of 186 policy and institutional events from 1957 to 2024, the article traces how IGiRD developed across four partially overlapping pathways: gender equality and anti-discrimination frameworks, women’s advancement in science and technology, health and medical research, and broader integration of sex and gender analysis across research fields and governance structures. Comparing the EU, US, Canada and South Korea, the analysis shows that IGiRD has not followed a single linear trajectory. The EU pathway is distinctive because gender mainstreaming became layered onto supranational research funding and evaluation structures, while North America demonstrates strong sectoral anchoring in health and biomedical research, and South Korea illustrates rapid formal-legal anchoring with incomplete operational embedding. The article contributes to historical-institutionalist science policy research by conceptualising IGiRD institutionalisation as layered, recursive and politically reversible. Formal anchoring in laws, strategies or funding rules matters, but durable change depends on operational embedding through review expertise, guidance, training, monitoring and feedback mechanisms, and on substantive methodological integration in research practice. This perspective clarifies why IGiRD can be stabilised, narrowed or reactivated under changing political conditions and offers policy implications for strengthening gender-sensitive R&I in emerging fields such as artificial intelligence.

Background Artificial intelligence (AI) for oral screening is usually judged by aggregate detection metrics on public benchmarks whose partitions, labels, and relevance to users are rarely checked. Methods We audited a prototype combining a YOLOv8m detector for six conditions (1,500 test images), a DenseNet169 histopathology network, and a ResNet18 router. Under a pre-specified plan, we measured duplication across partitions, tested removal of duplicated test images against 10,000 matched controls, compared duplicated copies' labels and predictions, compared the library versions, and ran every test image through the application pipeline. Results Near-duplicates of training images accounted for 17.3% of test and 17.1% of validation images (lower bounds). Removing duplicated test images changed mean average precision (mAP)@0.5 by +0.001 (95% confidence interval [CI] −0.012 to +0.014). Only 22% of duplicated photographs had identical labels on both copies; exploratory analysis suggested memorization of training labels in orientations seen in training. A library update moved mAP@0.5:0.95 by −0.012 with identical predictions. The router rejected 23% of in-domain photographs and 51% of photographs with ulcers, so ulcer sensitivity per image was 0.36 despite the highest benchmark recall (0.91). A class-mapping defect, still live in a public demonstration in September 2026, gave the wrong name to 73% of findings. The histopathology classifier classified every image as positive; its label was not a diagnosis. Conclusion Duplication compromised the benchmark's independence without detectably changing aggregate mAP; the defects that changed what was reported or displayed lay in the labels, evaluation software, and pipeline. Evaluations should verify partitions and labels, pin the library, and test deployed systems end to end.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence, sustainability reporting under IFRS S1 and S2, and digital tax administration are reshaping the accounting profession in Nigeria, yet there is little qualitative evidence on how the accountant’s role has changed or what competencies it now demands. This study explored the evolving role of the accountant in Nigeria through the lived experiences of senior practitioners. A qualitative phenomenological design was adopted. Twenty-five senior accountants with at least 15 years of post-qualification experience in Lagos, Abuja and Port Harcourt were purposively selected: 5 ICAN Fellows/Professors, 6 Big 4 and mid-tier audit partners, 8 industry CFOs and 6 public sector directors. Semi-structured interviews were conducted between January and May 2025, with saturation reached at the 21st interview. Data were analysed thematically using the Braun and Clarke framework with NVivo 12, collapsing 78 codes into four themes. A four-stage evolution model emerged: Bookkeeper (1990–2005), Financial Reporter (2006–2015), Digital Analyst (2016–2023) and Sustainability and AI Strategist (2024–date). Five future-ready competency domains were identified (technical accounting, taxation, audit and assurance, sustainability reporting, and soft and ethical skills), each cited by 80%–96% of participants. The main barriers were curriculum obsolescence (88%), technophobia (72%), cost and infrastructure (68%), absence of Nigerian emission factors (64%) and regulatory uncertainty (56%). A five-pillar framework spanning regulators, professional bodies, universities, corporate organisations and individual accountants is proposed to make Nigerian accountants future-ready and globally competitive.

Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing expectations for academic integrity in higher education, yet it remains unclear how institutional AI governance is translated into course-level guidance. This study examines how academic integrity and generative AI are framed in chemistry course documents and institutional policy documents. Using a hybrid inductive–deductive qualitative document analysis, I analyzed 18 publicly available chemistry course documents and 17 institutional policy documents from nine institutions across four countries. The analysis identified five higher-order themes in chemistry course documents: consequence-focused framing of academic integrity; academic integrity framed primarily as student responsibility; boilerplate policy language dominating over contextualized integrity guidance; generative AI addressed through silence, ambiguity, or prohibition; and faculty guidance and prevention rarely being explicit. A direct comparison revealed a substantial governance gap: 15 of 17 institutional policy documents (88.2%) explicitly mentioned generative AI, compared with only 2 of 18 chemistry course documents (11.1%). Institutional policies also more frequently addressed faculty guidance, research guidance, and AI governance than course documents. These findings suggest that institutional AI governance is developing more rapidly than its translation into chemistry course-level practice. Although policies and syllabi will continue to evolve as generative AI changes, the documented governance gap provides a baseline for examining how institution-level guidance is translated into instructional practice over time. The study concludes by proposing a coaching-oriented approach that shifts syllabus guidance from primarily punitive restrictions toward transparent, ethical, and pedagogically purposeful AI use.

The Linux command-line interface continues to serve as the primary control surface for software development, systems administration, and cloud operations, yet it executes instructions syntactically, without semantic awareness of user intent and without built-in mechanisms for diagnosing or repairing runtime failures. Over roughly the last decade, three largely distinct research communities have each addressed part of this problem: large language model (LLM)-based coding assistants embedded in integrated development environments (IDEs), natural-language-to-command translation systems that lower the barrier to shell usage, and operating-systems research on self-healing and autonomic computing that targets distributed and cloud infrastructure rather than the interactive terminal. This paper presents a structured, critical review of these three strands, together with the log-based anomaly-detection and AIOps literature that supplies much of the diagnostic machinery such systems would require. Literature was retained where it addressed semantic command interpretation, real-time or near-real-time failure diagnosis, autonomous or semi-autonomous recovery, or persistence of prior failure-resolution experience. The reviewed work is organized along four analytical dimensions — runtime integration, autonomy level, diagnostic depth, and knowledge retention — and compared qualitatively across these dimensions. The synthesis shows that autonomy and diagnostic sophistication increase substantially when moving from IDE assistants toward self-healing infrastructure research, but this increase is accompanied by a shift away from the single-operator, single-machine terminal context, and that no reviewed system combines real-time in-terminal diagnosis, multi-pathway recovery, and durable per-machine experiential learning while remaining confined to user space. The review further discusses recurring safety and governance themes — confidence-gated autonomy, privilege-aware execution, and explanation-first human oversight — that constrain the design space for any terminal-level orchestration layer, and it identifies four concrete research gaps together with a near-, mid-, and long-term research roadmap. The review does not claim that any single technology described is either novel or previously unstudied in isolation; its contribution is the cross-domain synthesis and the identification of the specific combination of properties that remains unaddressed.

Culturally embedded virtual games increasingly shape digital design, cultural communication, and place experience, yet how immersion translates into real-world engagement remains unclear. Drawing on the cognition–affect–conation model and flow theory, this study analyzes survey data from 458 young players. Presence, perceived realism, and curiosity significantly enhance emotional interaction and flow, while challenge improves flow but not emotional interaction. Flow mediates the relationship between virtual cultural experience and intention to visit real-world places; emotional interaction has no direct effect. Cultural identity strengthens the flow–participation relationship, highlighting its role in converting virtual immersion into cultural engagement. Culturally grounded games therefore function as destination pre-experience and cultural design platforms, through which digital scenes, cultural symbols, and interaction shape players’ imagination, identification, and willingness to participate in real-world cultural spaces. Findings inform game design, heritage communication, and place-experience design.

documents.abstract: Purpose This study opens the “psychological black box” of participation experiences in mass participation sport events (MPSEs) by examining how goal frames are associated with experiential outcomes through cognitive engagement and psychological empowerment. Drawing on goal-framing theory and the cognitive-affective processing system (CAPS), it proposes a process model linking goal frames to participation experiences, with social connectedness as a boundary condition. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative survey was conducted with participants in Taiwan who had engaged in non-elite sport events within the past year (N = 405). Data were analyzed using PLS-SEM with bootstrapping, employing established scales to measure goal framing, cognitive engagement, psychological empowerment, event enjoyment, subjective vitality, and social connectedness. Findings All three goal frames were positively associated with cognitive engagement and psychological empowerment. Cognitive engagement was positively associated with both event enjoyment and subjective vitality, whereas psychological empowerment was positively associated with subjective vitality but not event enjoyment. Social connectedness significantly moderated the relationship between psychological empowerment and subjective vitality, while the other moderation effects were not statistically significant. The indirect effects further revealed two distinct pathways, with cognitive engagement operating across both experiential outcomes and psychological empowerment being associated with subjective vitality. Originality/value This study advances a process-based perspective by integrating goal-framing theory with CAPS to explain how goal frames are associated with experiential outcomes through cognitive engagement and psychological empowerment. It demonstrates that social connectedness functions as a selective rather than universal boundary condition.

This independent analytical paper examines three major global challenges: biodiversity protection, the future of work in the age of artificial intelligence, and global supply chain resilience. Through the lens of project management, the paper explores the gap between global commitments and effective implementation, the unequal distribution of opportunities and resources, and the importance of accountability, education, and human empowerment. It argues that meaningful progress should be measured not only by stated goals, technological advances, or economic indicators, but also by tangible and lasting improvements in people's lives and opportunities. The paper reflects the author's personal perspective and applies project management principles to the analysis of complex global challenges.

Disaster risk is inherently spatial, yet geographic information systems (GIS) are still frequently used to end analysis at a classified hazard map rather than to support an engineering or operational decision. This critical review traces how GIS, integrated with remote sensing (RS), multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA), Web-GIS and geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI), has evolved across the disaster management cycle, and evaluates whether the resulting products are validated, uncertainty-aware and usable in civil-engineering practice. Twenty foundational studies (1992–2017) covering general emergency management, floods, earthquakes, landslides, cyclones and coastal hazards, drought and forest fire are appraised against a structured set of dimensions and are updated with recent systematic reviews of Web-GIS, AI/ML-enabled GIS, drone-based hazard sensing and AI-based landslide analysis. Four analytical families (knowledge-driven, data-driven, simulation-based and integrated Web-GIS/GeoAI) are compared. Knowledge-driven methods such as AHP and weighted overlay remain valuable where event inventories are scarce but are sensitive to expert-assigned weights; statistical and machine-learning models can improve prediction but are vulnerable to spatial leakage, non-representative inventories and limited interpretability; operational Web-GIS and GeoAI systems are advancing quickly but are rarely validated against independent events or evaluated by their effect on decisions. The most persistent gap is the translation of hazard classes into engineering quantities such as flood depth and velocity, design ground motion, slope safety factors, damage states and lifeline reliability. The review proposes (i) an eight-stage data-to-decision framework linking GIS, RS, GeoAI and engineering analysis, (ii) a minimum reporting and validation checklist for GIS-based hazard studies, and (iii) a prioritised research agenda covering multi-hazard modelling, near-real-time Web-GIS, uncertainty-aware GeoAI, digital twins, BIM–GIS integration and decision-centric validation.

Description Artificial intelligence is changing how people research, write, and communicate, raising important questions for the church and the work of the preacher. How can pastors benefit from emerging technologies without surrendering the personal study, prayer, theological judgment, and spiritual responsibility essential to faithful preaching? In From Legal Pads to Artificial Intelligence: How Technology Has Changed the Work of the Preacher—and What Must Never Change, Brent Madaris, D.Min., examines the relationship between technological assistance and the preacher’s personal responsibility in sermon preparation. Drawing on pastoral ministry, theological study, and professional experience in healthcare, the author considers both the potential benefits and the limitations of artificial intelligence in vocational ministry. The essay distinguishes between using AI as a tool for research, organization, and refinement and allowing it to substitute for the preacher’s own biblical study, spiritual reflection, theological discernment, and pastoral judgment. It also considers how lessons from the responsible use of AI in clinical practice may inform discussions about its use in ministry. Rather than offering an unqualified endorsement or rejection of artificial intelligence, this work argues for thoughtful and responsible engagement with emerging technology while maintaining the convictions and practices that must remain central to Christian preaching. AI may assist in preparing a sermon, but it cannot prepare the preacher. This essay is intended for pastors, ministry leaders, theological educators, students, and others interested in preaching, Christian ministry, theological reflection, and the ethical use of artificial intelligence. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; sermon preparation; preaching; pastoral ministry; Christian ministry; theological education; Christian ethics; technology and religion; responsible AI use.

Designing power electronics converters traditionally requires intensive human expertise across topology sizing, commercial component selection, circuit simulation verification, and schematic drafting. While Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise in electronic design automation (EDA), applying standalone LLMs directly to board-level power electronics schematic synthesis suffers from severe engineering hallucinations, including inaccurate analytical sizing, fabricated or mismatched component part numbers, violated voltage derating margins, and broken topological connectivity. In this paper, we propose a Bounded Dual-Loop Automated Schematic Synthesis Framework that translates natural language specifications into verified, editable KiCad schematics and manufacturing deliverables. Our workflow integrates six stages across three functional columns: (1) requirement parsing and knowledge-driven power stage synthesis covering non-isolated (Buck, Boost) and isolated/resonant (Flyback, DAB, half-bridge LLC) topologies; (2) contract- and evidence-coordinated component selection grounded in distributor APIs and OEM datasheets, coupled with closed-loop ngspice transient verification and stress feedback; and (3) modular control hardware integration and multi-format deliverable generation featuring native KiCad netlist round-trip verification. End-to-end case studies on a 24-36V to 12V,2A Buck converter (29 positions, 83 verified terminals) and an isolated 48V to 24V, 0.5A, Dual-Active Bridge (DAB) converter (87 positions, 341 verified terminals), alongside comparative evaluations against a Vanilla LLM baseline, demonstrate that our framework improves component verification coverage from 22.2 to 98.6, nominal value consistency from 0 to 97.7, and SPICE simulation pass rates from 0 to 100.

Dumper, tipper and haul-truck operations in opencast mines expose workers to high-consequence hazards arising from vehicle mass, restricted visibility, mixed traffic, changing haul roads, dumping edges and human performance. This study develops an implementable risk-assessment framework that translates Indian mine-safety requirements and international evidence into operational controls and verification routines. A purposive integrative review of official DGMS, MSHA and NIOSH material and peer-reviewed research was combined with examination of the supplied risk-assessment-based safe operating procedure. The search was not systematic, and no incident-level dataset or formal quality appraisal was available. Sources were mapped to operating phase, hazard, control, verification, accountable role and learning indicator. The proposed framework covers six operating phases and six control domains. It assigns task HIRA to baseline screening, JSA/JHA to detailed high-risk steps, Bowtie to fatal-event pathways and critical controls, and FMEA/FMECA to equipment failure modes. It also specifies five verification modes and links critical controls to failure responses, owners and prospective indicators. The framework is sufficiently specified for site adaptation and prospective pilot evaluation; it has not been tested as an intervention or empirically validated.

This systematic review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) shapes the digital experiences of young users through social media reels and personalized content. The study focuses on the ethical dimensions of these developments, addressing concerns such as algorithmic bias, data privacy, exposure to potentially harmful content, and the broader psychological effects on adolescents. This paper evaluates current literature to uncover the ethical tensions between personalization and manipulation. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, this review systematically analysed 42 peer-reviewed articles and industry reports published between 2015 and 2024. The analysis highlights how AI's profit-driven logic reinforces compulsive behaviours, body image concerns, and social comparison among adolescents. Such effects are particularly pronounced among adolescents, who are in a critical stage of identity formation and are more vulnerable to the psychological consequences of digital exposure. To address these challenges, the paper proposes a multi-stakeholder ethical framework designed to promote algorithmic transparency, empower young users through digital literacy, and enhance regulatory accountability. This framework emphasizes the shared responsibility of technology companies, policymakers, educators, and guardians in mitigating the adverse impacts of AI-driven personalization. The review's insights hold significant relevance for those seeking to balance innovation with ethical safeguards in the evolving landscape of youth, technology, and social media.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract In this viewpoint, we present our perspective—informed by published evidence and by our own work on AI-driven digital health systems—on why AI has had limited real-world impact in preventive health and how it should be redesigned. Most AI systems in health care are built as episodic prediction tools, whereas preventive care depends on sustained behavioral change; the consequences are visible in consistently high attrition and low long-term adherence across digital health interventions. The aim of this viewpoint is to argue that this failure is structural rather than incremental and to propose an integrated, interaction-centric alternative. We advance 3 key messages. First, the limited impact of AI in preventive health reflects a structural misalignment between episodic, prediction-centric system design and the longitudinal dynamics of health behavior. Second, addressing this misalignment requires treating continuous interaction as the primary unit of design, which we articulate through a behavioral informatics framework integrating 6 interdependent layers: data, knowledge, reasoning, interaction, behavior, and governance. The contribution of this framework is explicitly integrative: it synthesizes previously separate strands, including just-in-time adaptive interventions, behavioral intervention technologies, and human-AI interaction research, into a single system-level account. Third, evaluation must shift from predictive accuracy and short-term engagement toward measurable behavioral trajectories and longitudinal outcomes, with explicit attention to feasibility and to conditions under which simpler, non-AI interventions remain preferable. This viewpoint is addressed to digital health researchers and AI developers, behavioral scientists, clinicians involved in preventive care, and policymakers responsible for governing continuously interacting AI systems.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Editorial Taking up the role of Managing Editor of the Journal of Interventional Epidemiology and Public Health (JIEPH) is both a privilege and a call to stewardship. I take over from Dr Sheba Nakacubo Gitta, who served as JIEPH’s Managing Editor until December 2025. My experience within the Journal’s editorial leadership, first as Deputy Managing Editor from October 2024 to December 2025 and then as Acting Managing Editor from January to September 2026, taught me firsthand how much this Journal owes to the people around it. It is with that appreciation that I approach this first editorial in my new role. JIEPH was launched in November 2018 in Maputo, Mozambique, during the 7th AFENET Scientific Conference, as an online, open-access, peer-reviewed scientific journal published by the African Field Epidemiology Network (AFENET) [1]. It has since grown into an open-access journal that publishes contextually relevant evidence from Africa and beyond, without charging article processing or submission fees and letting authors retain copyright through a Creative Commons Attribution license [2]. These foundations, laid by the journal’s founders, publishers, previous and current editorial leaders, authors, reviewers, readers and institutional partners, are what we build on today. Where we stand Publication output has grown substantially. In 2024, JIEPH published 77 articles: 57 regular articles, 10 in the Rwanda Field Epidemiology Training Programme supplement, and 10 in the first volume of the 8th AFENET Scientific Conference supplement [3]. In 2025, it published 149 articles: 105 regular articles and 44 supplement articles covering Togo FETP, Sierra Leone FETP and Volume 2 of the eighth AFENET Scientific Conference supplement [3]. As of mid-October 2026, Volume 9 carries 170 regular articles and 34 supplement articles, a combined total of 204. The journal has cumulatively published 15 supplements and eight conference proceedings [4]. Recent supplements and proceedings include contributions from the Guinea and Uganda Field Epidemiology Training Programmes, the 2nd ECOWAS Lassa fever regional conference, and AFENET @20 commemorative special issues [3]. These figures demonstrate increased publishing activity; the next challenge is to translate that growth into sustained scientific quality and evidence use. JIEPH’s visibility has grown alongside its publication output. The journal was added to the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) in April 2025 [2]. JIEPH’s indexing and abstracting coverage includes Scopus, CABI Global Health and CAB Abstracts; it also has a SCImago journal profile and is discoverable through EBSCOhost [5,6]. My ambition for JIEPH’s next stage is to build a global home for interventional epidemiology and public health, rooted in Africa’s field epidemiology community. Researchers and practitioners anywhere should be able to turn to the journal for rigorous, practice-relevant evidence on outbreaks, surveillance, public health programmes and population health. The central question is therefore no longer simply how much we can publish, but how we strengthen the quality, visibility, influence, inclusiveness and sustainability of what we publish, and how that evidence moves into practice. Four connected priorities will guide this phase: expanding indexation and discoverability, improving scientific and public health impact, nurturing the next generation of scientists, and building a sustainable journal. Becoming a global home is the ambition that connects these priorities, rather than a separate objective. Scientific quality, research integrity, editorial independence and responsible publishing will underpin them all. Expanding global visibility and discoverability Researchers, public health institutions and programmes in Africa and around the world continue to generate valuable evidence through outbreak investigations, surveillance, epidemiological studies, laboratory systems, programme implementation and community interventions. Publishing that evidence is not enough if researchers, practitioners, policymakers and communities, in any country, find it hard to discover and use. JIEPH is indexed in the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) and African Journals Online (AJOL). Its content and metadata are also discoverable through Google Scholar, OpenAlex, Scilit and OpenAIRE, with Crossref supporting metadata dissemination [5]. Sustaining and extending this visibility is the next task. Respondents to the 2026 half-year post-publication author survey identified broader coverage in databases such as PubMed and Web of Science as an important priority [7]. Inclusion in indexing services is decided by external bodies and cannot be secured by aspiration alone. JIEPH will therefore concentrate on what lies within its control: consistently meeting the scientific, editorial, ethical, technical and publishing standards that wider indexation requires, including complete article metadata and timely publication. Our aim is not merely to enter more databases but to be a journal whose quality, consistency, transparency and reliability merit sustained inclusion. Moving from publication to practice Authors see JIEPH as a natural home for field-based public health work. In a post-publication survey conducted between 26 June and 1 July 2026, 25 authors from 15 countries across West, East, Central and Southern Africa reported a mean overall satisfaction of 8.9 out of 10. The mean likelihood of recommending JIEPH was 9.4 out of 10 and of submitting again 9.3 out of 10. Importantly, 88% said that publishing in JIEPH had enhanced the visibility of their work [7]. That reach already extends beyond the continent. Recent articles include a molecular surveillance study from a state public health laboratory in Mexico [8], and a commentary from the World Health Organization’s Health Emergencies Programme in Geneva, Switzerland, on our Sierra Leone mpox cohort study, which presents that experience as a model for preparedness in Africa and globally [9]. A review of mobile public health emergency operations centres by an author based in the United States with a co-author at Africa CDC, has drawn nearly 9,000 views on the journal website [10]. Authors in India have published a study of carbonated beverage knowledge and practice among medical students in Kerala [11], and authors in Pakistan a letter on over-the-counter medicine and antibiotic misuse [12], while authors from Yemen’s Field Epidemiology Training Program and national AFP surveillance programme have reported ten years of acute flaccid paralysis surveillance data from Sana’a [13]. Together these show a journal whose subjects extend from outbreak response to non-communicable diseases and antimicrobial resistance. These findings encourage us, and they also challenge us to define impact more ambitiously. Readership, citation and inclusion in evidence syntheses matter, but bibliometrics alone cannot capture a public health journal’s contribution. For JIEPH, the larger question is whether evidence strengthens surveillance, improves outbreak preparedness and response, informs programmes and policy, guides resource allocation, supports teaching and training, and ultimately contributes to better population health, in Africa and wherever the work is used. The proposed public health emergency management curriculum published in the journal illustrates the kind of practice-oriented contribution we seek [14]. Our immediate contribution will be to encourage submissions that pair scientific rigour with clear relevance to public health action. We will ask authors, reviewers and editors to make three points explicit: what was found, why it matters, and how it could inform practice. Lessons from interventional epidemiology in African settings, including outbreak response under resource constraints, are relevant to health systems everywhere, and we want them to travel. We therefore need to ask not only how often articles are cited, but whether they are read, discussed, taught, translated into programmes and used in decisions. These steps can support evidence use; demonstrating changes in programmes, policy or population health will require evidence beyond publication metrics. Publication should be the beginning of scientific engagement, not its end. Nurturing the next generation of scientists Capacity development has long been part of JIEPH’s identity. Since 2021, the journal has hosted quarterly scientific-writing webinars and supported podcasts, workshops, French-language access and resources for researchers and authors [15]. The author survey provides encouraging feedback on editorial experience: professionalism of editorial communication and fairness of peer review each received a 96% positive rating, and respondents reported that reviewers helped improve the methodology, clarity and discussion of their manuscript [7]. These findings support the value of constructive editorial engagement and suggest that the developmental approach is reaching its intended audience. Our ambition is therefore twofold: to provide a platform for excellent science from Africa and the world, and to help develop the people who produce, review, communicate and use that science. Developing scientific capacity begins with making standards explicit, applying them consistently, and giving feedback that strengthens authors’ methods, reporting and interpretation. It also requires a growing community of skilled reviewers, editors, statistical advisers and publication professionals from Africa and across the world. Reviewer development, mentorship and early-career editorial opportunities can help build that community. Continuing education can strengthen the use of appropriate reporting guidelines, responsible artificial intelligence and publication ethics, alongside scientific writing. Purpose This paper aims to systematically synthesize state-of-the-art advancements in wearable cuffless blood pressure (BP) monitoring technologies, critically examining the sensing hardware, estimation algorithms and calibration strategies and identifying the core barriers that impede the translation from laboratory prototypes to clinically reliable cardiovascular monitoring systems. Design/methodology/approach This paper adopts a comprehensive literature review approach, systematically analyzing emerging sensing modalities – including optoelectronic (PPG), mechanoelectric (triboelectric, piezoelectric, piezoresistive), ultrasonic and multimodal fusion systems – alongside the evolutionary trajectory of BP estimation techniques, from mechanism-driven models (PTT/PWV) through data-driven deep learning to the emerging physics-informed artificial intelligence paradigm. Clinical validation frameworks and calibration strategies are also critically assessed. Findings The review reveals that while significant progress has been made in sensor sensitivity, signal processing and algorithmic accuracy, several critical barriers persist before widespread clinical adoption. These include motion-induced signal degradation, limited cross-population generalizability of algorithms, the absence of standardized validation protocols for cuffless devices and calibration drift over time. Physics-informed AI emerges as a promising paradigm for improving robustness, interpretability and generalization by embedding hemodynamic constraints into data-driven models. Research limitations/implications As a review paper, the findings are based on published literature rather than original experimental data. Future research should focus on adaptive calibration frameworks, rigorous multi-scenario validation aligned with ESH 2023 recommendations and hardware-software co-design approaches. Practical implications The review provides actionable guidance for researchers, clinicians, and device developers by identifying key technological bottlenecks and outlining future directions, including endogenous autonomous calibration benchmarks and multimodal sensing integration, to accelerate the development of clinically viable wearable BP monitoring systems. Originality/value This paper uniquely bridges the gap between sensing hardware and clinical requirements by providing an integrated analysis across the full technology chain – from sensors to algorithms to clinical translation. It highlights physics-informed AI as a critical emerging direction and proposes a forward-looking framework for all-scenario adaptive dynamic calibration, offering a comprehensive roadmap for the field.

Purpose: Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) remain a major clinical and economic burden, and early detection of transmission clusters is essential for timely intervention. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) is the reference standard for outbreak confirmation, but its cost, turnaround time, and operational requirements limit its use as an always-on first-line surveillance tool. Because matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) spectra are already generated during routine species identification, they may provide a rapid triage layer before confirmatory sequencing. Methods: We synthesize current evidence for artificial intelligence (AI)-based MALDI-TOF MS analysis in within-species typing, strain relatedness inference, and outbreak-oriented surveillance. We organize the literature into three methodological pathways: peak-centric biomarker typing, supervised subtype classification, and representation learning. Results: The available evidence indicates that AI-based models can extract within-species signals from MALDI-TOF MS spectra that are relevant to typing and outbreak surveillance, but performance remains context-dependent. Peak-based approaches offer interpretability but are vulnerable to spectral instability and limited portability. Supervised classifiers can perform well for narrow predefined targets, but depend on fixed label spaces and may degrade when local epidemiology changes. Representation-learning approaches are less clinically validated for typing, but may offer the most scalable route toward adaptable, similarity-based early-warning systems. Conclusions: MALDI-TOF MS should not be viewed as a replacement for WGS, but as a locally calibrated decision-support tool that prioritizes suspicious isolates for sequencing and infection prevention and control (IPC) review, similar to a screening tool. Future studies should move beyond retrospective accuracy estimates and evaluate prospective clinical utility, including time gained, sequencing saved, false-alert burden, portability to new laboratories, and performance after minimal local calibration.

Artificial intelligence in diabetes care has historically relied on task-specific supervised learning, such as bespoke networks for retinopathy grading, kidney disease prediction, and glucose forecasting. The emergence of foundation models (FMs: large models pretrained on broad data, typically with self-supervision, and adapted to many downstream tasks) is displacing this paradigm across diabetes-relevant modalities: ophthalmic models such as RETFound, pretrained on 1.6 million retinal photographs, have been reported to outperform task-specific networks on retinopathy grading and systemic disease prediction, especially when labeled data are scarce; transformer-based time-series models are replacing long short-term memory (LSTM) pipelines for continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) forecasting; clinical large language models (LLMs) such as Med-PaLM and GPT-4 attain expert-level scores on medical question-answering benchmarks; and generative models supply synthetic CGM and electronic health record (EHR) data. This review provides a critical, modality-organized synthesis of this transition. We (i) formalize a three-era taxonomy: rule-based risk scores (era I), task-specific deep learning (era II, 2016–2020), and foundation models (era III, from 2021), and map the diabetes literature onto it; (ii) survey foundation-model architectures, pretraining objectives, and adaptation strategies across retinal imaging, CGM, longitudinal EHR, and multimodal data; (iii) expose an evaluation crisis: benchmark contamination of LLM medical evaluations, a near-universal absence in the literature we reviewed of external and prospective validation for retinal and CGM foundation models, miscalibration under dataset shift, and, to our knowledge and within the reviewed literature (January 2016–December 2025; negative findings are time-sensitive), the absence of any randomized evaluation of a foundation model in a diabetes workflow; and (iv) analyze safety risks: hallucinated insulin-dosing advice, automation bias, inherited algorithmic inequity, and privacy exposure during adaptation. We conclude that the decisive open problem is no longer representation learning but grounded, calibrated, causally informed deployment, requiring contamination-resistant evaluation, prospective trials, and hybrid architectures coupling foundation-model representations with treatment-effect estimation.
