documents.abstract: Introduction The movement of generative artificial intelligence from still-image to moving-image creation has reshaped the symbolic mechanism of human-AI co-creation. Methods This comparative observational study asks how prompt expression changes when the output shifts from static images to moving images, comparing two large-scale public prompt corpora under one neural topic-modeling protocol that combines lexical analysis of style, quality, technical, motion, camera, and format vocabulary with manual family coding and validity checks, and adds an exploratory user-focused topic structure. Results Video prompts weaken the style, quality, and technical decoration characteristic of image prompts and instead organize meaning around action, scene, and screen format. Because the corpora differ in platform ecology, model generation, period, and corpus construction as well as in modality, these differences are described rather than causally attributed, and the format result is the most interface-sensitive of them. Artist-style imitation loses its earlier prominence, a decline that survives the coding reliability checks, while everyday action and scene description forms the largest family in the adjudicated solution, a position that is sensitive to those checks. Discussion Prompting practice moved from selecting aesthetic styles toward specifying how a scene moves and how it is framed, and the prompting grammar observed here appears bound to the modality and the period. The terms that organized image prompts did not carry over intact to video prompts. These patterns suggest that the symbolic interface of human-AI co-creation is not a fixed grammar but an adaptive arrangement that responds to the salient capabilities of a generative system. The study contributes a comparative account of how the division of creative labor is reconfigured across media modalities, with implications for co-creation theory, generative interface design, and media literacy education.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) settles into everyday practices of inquiry, an old epistemological question returns in a new guise: when does a proposition a user takes from an AI output become something the user knows, and when is it rational to trust it as such? This paper argues that the characteristic failures of AI-mediated inquiry are precisely those that the justified-true-belief (JTB) tradition and its post-Gettier anti-luck refinements were built to diagnose, and it advances three claims. First, AI outputs inherit neither the presumptive warrant of testimony nor the reliabilist warrant of deterministic tools: unaudited trust in a calculator rests on a type-level reliability record, and for general-purpose generative models there is no type-stable process to which such a record could attach -- a practical form of the generality problem. Second, use that stops at obtaining an output turns generative AI into a Gettier machine: the user's fluency-based seeming of justification is disconnected from the truth of what is believed, and, as a clock running ten times too fast illustrates, sheer speed of production multiplies coincidental hits, inflating the appearance of reliability without improving the standing of any single hit. Third, the remedy is a three-step structure of use -- acquisition, understanding, independent verification -- whose first two steps answer to the classical belief and justification conditions and whose third answers to the post-Gettier sensitivity condition. The result is a stakes-indexed criterion of rational trust, justified true output (JTO), with an everyday test: "Had this been false, would I have noticed?" The criterion is defended against objections from over-demandingness, the extended mind, model improvement, and redundancy.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Previous uses of Universal Design (UD) in handicraft products have focused mainly on evaluation, identifying how products do not meet the seven principles of UD, rather than offering practical redesign suggestions or empirical evidence to support improvements. To overcome this shortcoming, this study proposes a design-based approach that integrates the Craft Universality Taxonomy (CUT) and the Participatory Redesign Protocol (PRP) to assess, redesign, and validate the universality of handicraft products without compromising their cultural authenticity. The study builds upon existing inclusive design and co-design research, which proposes the seven UD principles as moving, culturally based parameters instead of static evaluations. The two-stage identification process, consisting of a cross-domain design survey (n = 31) and a craft-specific Delphi panel (n = 30), was used to rank and classify 10 vital universality attributes using the Relative Importance Index (RII) and the Kano model. They are grouped into four dimensions: (1) Functional Usability, (2) Cultural Legibility, (3) Adaptive Flexibility and (4) Economic Accessibility, a dimension not featured in any previous UD frameworks, identified by the craft domain experts as being a near-baseline condition for handicraft universality. The PRP was applied to two traditional Indian handicraft products (bamboo/cane stool and Moojh grass basket) through a structured co-creation process involving practising artisans and the craft-specific expert panel (n = 30). Ten attributes were rated on a Likert scale to determine baseline universality scores based on the CUT. Redesign interventions were co-created with artisans under a Cultural Integrity Boundary Condition that did not involve changing the fundamental craft process, primary material, or symbolic identity. A Universality Gain Index (UGI) was used to compare pre- and post-assessment expert scores, quantifying improvements at both the attribute and dimension levels and allowing a replicable measure of gains in inclusivity for craft-based products. The results indicate that "universality" in handicraft design does not belong to the attributes of the object itself but is the result of informed, iterative redesign. Gains were greatest for the stool on ergonomics and adaptability (UGI 64% and 60% respectively), and for the basket on affordability (UGI 57%), lending further credence to this attribute's status as a critical "must-be" feature whose absence most clearly signals dissatisfaction. The framework treats universality as a field transformation rather than a homogenisation of the universal, in which usability and cultural relevance are treated as adaptive intensifications. The study provides a replicable and scalable toolkit for designers, artisans and policymakers, illustrating how Universal Design principles can be integrated into craft-based practice with measurable, evidence-based results that help preserve cultural heritage while increasing market access.

Personal accessories are undergoing a profound transformation, driven by the integration of adaptive smart technology, that are expanding both their functional capabilities and symbolic significance. As artefacts, they are both utilitarian tools and material expressions of cultural identity. Among many existing frameworks, most of the contemporary universal design models address only singular dimensions like ergonomics, usability, or cultural symbolism. No existing validated multidimensional assessment framework fulfils the conditions of functional universality, socio-cultural inclusivity, technological accessibility, and ethical sustainability together. A systematic review of more than twenty published models of universal design (UD) confirms this lacuna and shows that existing frameworks are mainly unidimensional, Western-centric, and structurally inadequate for evaluating today's smart accessory ecosystems. This paper presents the FSTE (Functional, Socio-Cultural, Technological, Ethical-Sustainability) Framework as the first empirically validated (through expert and user pilot study) multidimensional evaluation instrument for assessing the universality of personal accessories. The framework was developed through expert Delphi validation (n = 15; α = 0.87; κ = 0.81) and a user pilot study (n = 15 users across three product categories); user pilot study confirmed discriminant validity across product types (D1 mean = 3.95; D2 = 3.53; D3 = 3.57; D4 = 3.77). The FSTE comprises four dimensions, nine parameters, and twenty-seven measurable indicators.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: Over the past century, public education has used the “factory model” to prepare students, a mindset that originates from Industrial Revolution-era reforms. Recent reform movements, such as No Child Left Behind, sought to optimize the factory model without considering new directions. This chapter introduces the concept of reimagining, rather than reforming, our schools. Reimagining education allows for dramatic changes in the structure of public education. The future needs of today’s students are dramatically different to what they were when the factory model of schooling emerged. To respond to student needs, educational leaders must develop futures-literate leadership skills. Futures-literate leaders accept and embrace change, regardless of inherent uncertainty (i.e., the emergence of generative AI technology). This chapter assists the reader by reflecting on the importance of reimagining schools, the reader’s preparedness to lead with a futures-literate mindset, and identifying areas for growth in reimagining.

As artificial intelligence (AI) gains an increasing role in the way people form emotional bonds with technology, this work specifically explores the gendered aspects of trust, vulnerability, and emotional bonding in human-AI relationships among a sample of students in a higher education environment. A cross-sectional quantitative study was conducted on 210 undergraduate and postgraduate students in the Vellore district, Tamil Nadu, India, using convenience sampling method. The results showed that gender was found to be a strong but inconsistent predictor of the behaviors in AI interactions and there were no significant differences in trust and emotional attachment. Age and field of study also had no significant effects. Students generally reported moderate levels of trust and attachment, which suggests a cautious, optimistic approach toward Artificial Intelligence. This study highlights gender as an important factor in disclosure behavior while broader demographic factors remain less influential.

The application of Generative AI is reshaping students’ learning. However, student motivation in GenAI-supported learning is complex and influenced by multiple factors. To fully realize the educational potential of GenAI, a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between student motivation and GenAI is necessary. To address this gap, this study conducted a systematic literature review. From the perspective of Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this review examined 39 articles published between 2023 and 2025, drawn from two databases: Web of Science and Scopus. This study provides three major findings. First, competence-related learning activities were the most frequently identified across the reviewed studies. Second, four categories were reported in relation to student motivation: GenAI characteristics, learner factors, psychological factors, and environmental factors. Third, three major aspects of motivational conceptualization are basic psychological needs, motivation construct, and motivation-related construct. In addition, quantitative questionnaires were the dominant approach used to measure these constructs. Finally, the relationship among these three findings is illustrated. The findings provide insights into student motivation in GenAI-supported learning and highlight the relevance of GenAI characteristics, learners, and the learning environment. This study also provides theoretical and practical implications for facilitating students’ motivation in GenAI-supported learning environments.

Pain assessment in older adults with cognitive impairment remains challenging, particularly when changes in communication make self-report difficult. Validated observational tools, caregiver and staff knowledge, clinical examination, and repeated within-person assessment remain the foundation of care. However, information from these sources may be incomplete, conflicting, or documented across different settings. Generative artificial intelligence (AI), including large language models, may help clinicians organize and review this information, but it should not independently detect, diagnose, or determine treatment for pain. In this Perspective article, we propose a person-centered, clinician-governed framework for the bounded use of generative AI in pain assessment. The framework organizes seven testable use cases under three core functions: capacity-sensitive elicitation, source-attributed synthesis, and longitudinal support and communication. Potential applications include adaptive pain interviews, identification of possible pain-related information in everyday language, structuring of behavioral observations, multi-informant synthesis, synthesis of validated nonverbal indicators, longitudinal pain-related diaries, and caregiver communication support. Each application requires clear limits, source identification, communication of uncertainty, consideration of alternative causes of distress, and mandatory clinician verification before clinical action or documentation. We also examine risks related to suggestibility, bias, medication effects, privacy, alert fatigue, workload, and overreliance on AI-generated outputs. A five-step research pathway is proposed that includes co-design, technical testing, clinical validation, evaluation across populations and care settings, and risk-based governance. Generative AI should be adopted only if prospective studies demonstrate meaningful value beyond validated assessment methods and usual clinical workflows without reducing patient choice, replacing clinical judgment, or increasing workload.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The article critically interrogates why the build-out of generative “AI” in the ideological-material form it has taken in the USA can be viewed as symptomatic of the intensifying polycrisis of US digital capitalism and the US-led neo-imperial order. Employing a neo-Luddite-Marxist approach to analyse the technology of GenAI, first the eugenic-eschatological ideological underpinnings of it are examined, along with the central problematic, ecologically unsustainable technical characteristic of its development and functioning and the politico-economic conditions of its possibility which make it a symptom of the polycrisis. The second focus is the centrality of GenAI in digital capitalism’s mutation to become an even more speculative, unsustainable, environment- and society-destructive, power-centralising and worker-exploiting form – ‘Muskism’, that is parasitically dependent on the US state. Finally, it tackles the role of GenAI in the implementation of the end-times fascist project of the second Trump Administration and its deliberate escalation of the polycrisis. Keywords: AI, end-times fascism, digital capitalism, Muskism, Trump, polycrisis.

Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs) have advanced from rule-based learning environments to adaptive systems that use artificial intelligence techniques, modelling of learners and learning analytics. The wide range of systems and learning approaches makes it difficult to understand how learner data is mapped to adaptive instructional decision making. This paper reports a systematic literature review of pedagogical alignment, adaptivity, and analytics in Intelligent Tutoring Systems. This review synthesises relevant research in three inter-related dimensions of ITS design: pedagogical alignment (how tutoring strategies and learning objectives are aligned); adaptivity (how systems respond to learners' characteristics knowledge behaviour and performance); and learning analytics (how learners’ data are captured, analysed, and applied). The review mostly focuses on the integration of knowledge tracing, student modelling, educational data mining, learning analytics, and AI-based tutoring technologies in adaptive learning; it discusses the effectiveness of different adaptive learning processes; evaluation approaches; and technical and pedagogical issues related to adaptive learning (including data quality, data sparsity interpretability individualization, scalability, and model-to-pedagogy complementarity). The integration of the points of view presented in this study helps to provide a comprehensive view of the relationship between the data analyses adaptive decisions, and pedagogy used in intelligent tutoring systems. The review aims to lay a conceptual foundation for building adaptive ITSs that are more sensitive to individual learner needs, are informed by data, and are pedagogically consistent in their teaching strategies, and to suggest future research directions for the architecture of integrated adaptive ITSs in different educational settings.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) now lets people turn verbal self-descriptions into visual self-representations, creating a new setting for studying self-concept clarity (SCC) in human–AI interaction. We tested whether generative AI-assisted self-visualization (GAISV) was associated with higher short-term SCC through cognitive mirroring rather than through general immersive flow, and whether this depends on how far participants identify with the generated image. We introduce the AI Mirror Self-Integration Model and evaluated it in two stages. A pilot study (124 valid participants) examined the Cognitive Mirroring in Human-AI Self-Visualization Scale (CM-HAIS) and supported its use as a task-state measure of reflective self-processing. A randomized main experiment then recruited 328 valid participants. Primary analyses compared three conditions—GAISV, active non-self image generation, and passive image viewing ( N = 246)—with SCC measured immediately after the task and again 48–72 h later (T2 N = 216). A self-description-only condition was retained as an exploratory comparison and was not part of the primary tests. GAISV produced higher post-task and follow-up SCC than both control conditions. In parallel mediation models, the GAISV effect was primarily associated with cognitive mirroring rather than with flow, and the cognitive-mirroring indirect path was stronger than the flow path immediately after the task. Image self-identification was associated with the strength of the cognitive-mirroring path at the post-task assessment, as indicated by the index of moderated mediation; the follow-up moderation evidence was weaker. AI-generated self-images were therefore not clarifying by default. GAISV was associated with higher short-term SCC primarily when the image was experienced as personally identifying and engaged reflective cognitive mirroring rather than mere immersion. Condition differences were statistically reliable but small (Cohen’s d ≈ 0.21–0.27), and the mediation results are mechanism-consistent associations rather than evidence of causal ordering.

Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is changing how young people access cultural knowledge and understand sociocultural narratives. Some research has examined the information risks of Generative AI (GenAI), but few have studied how young people from different cultural backgrounds perceive and are affected by these risks. Based on the interviews conducted with 33 university students in Shenzhen from Guangdong, Hong Kong and Macao, this paper conducts thematic analysis and cross-background comparison of their views on risks to cultural information, strategies for identity negotiation and related sociocultural experiences. Based on the above analysis, the three main topics are: (1) the three perceived risks: information distortion, cultural misrepresentation and information homogenization; (2) the three identity negotiation strategies in response to AI-generated cultural information: identity affirmation, identity reconsideration and identity defense; and (3) associations of language use, platform exposure and cross-regional cultural experiences with different interpretations and responses to cultural information by participants. Based on the data in this paper, it has been determined that participants' previous cultural experiences are incorporated into their perception and response of AI-generated cultural materials; therefore, this study will provide specific evidence to help improve the critical evaluation of cultural information and digital literacy education for young people in the Greater Bay Area.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence and large language models has dramatically altered the landscape of digital communications. Although these new tools have made possible significant improvements in language generation and understanding, they have also increased the scalability, customization, and contextual sophistication of cyberbullying. Modern cyberbullying has also evolved from being merely a matter of using language that is hurtful and insulting to the use of computer automation and language-generation capabilities on the internet. Cyber-bullying cannot be categorized under a simplistic classification scheme but has to be envisioned as an interactional, dynamic, socio-cognitive process entailing implicit intentionality, emotions, and escalation mechanisms. Challenged by the limitations of reactive, punitive systems, this chapter unfolds the paradigm shift to generative empathic moderation (GEM), with AI performing an active virtual mediation role. Bringing together generative models, explainable AI, and human oversight, GEM seeks to diffuse toxic interactions and induce de-escalation while ensuring the reconciliation of operational optimality, responsibility, and social acceptability.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This paper develops generative invitation as a provisional description of relational praxis in which an addressed offering enters another participant’s historically situated activity. It distinguishes affordances, offerings, recipient uptake, counterproposal, immediate achievement, and possible changes in effective opportunities or enduring capacities. Buber, Levinas, Ricœur, Arendt, ecological affordance theory, educational scaffolding, participatory sense-making, and literary reception provide substantial philosophical precedents. The generative-relational (GR) proposal is therefore evaluated for its incremental usefulness in tracing the relation between an offering, heterogeneous receiving conditions, subsequent trajectories, and control over enabling resources. Constructed cases from aesthetics, education, interspecies encounters, and human–AI interaction illustrate both this possible scope and the differing evidence required for claims about experience, autonomy, and agency. A comparative account tests whether established theories already explain the same observations, and distinguishes productive influence from ethical legitimacy or entitlement to resulting value. Conceptual discrimination, explanatory adequacy, and normative accountability provide three separate tests of this account. Its immediate contribution is a set of revisable distinctions; whether they jointly identify an explanatory mechanism beyond existing theories remains a question for comparative and empirical inquiry.

Inflammation is a complex biological defense response to infection, tissue injury, and other danger signals, playing a fundamental role in maintaining tissue homeostasis and immune balance. A well-regulated and transient inflammatory response facilitates pathogen clearance, limits tissue damage, and promotes tissue repair. However, when inflammatory responses become persistent, dysregulated, or fail to resolve appropriately, they may progress to chronic inflammation, thereby contributing to the initiation and progression of numerous major diseases, including autoimmune disorders, metabolic diseases, cardiovascular diseases, and cancer. Chronic inflammation is not merely characterized by sustained elevation of inflammatory mediators; rather, it represents a complex systemic process involving immune cell reprogramming, disruption of tissue barrier integrity, aberrant tissue repair, metabolic reprogramming, and remodeling of the tissue microenvironment. Accumulating evidence from genetic studies has demonstrated that inter-individual variability in the magnitude of inflammatory responses and susceptibility to inflammatory diseases is, at least in part, attributable to genetic variation within the human genome. Genetic polymorphisms encompass single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), insertion/deletion variants (InDels), copy number variations (CNVs), and more complex structural variants. These genetic variants can influence inflammatory responses at multiple levels by modulating gene expression, RNA processing, protein structure and function, antigen presentation, intracellular signal transduction, and immune cell function, thereby shaping individual sensitivity and responsiveness to inflammatory stimuli. Among the numerous genetic loci implicated in inflammatory diseases, the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) region, cytokine-encoding genes, pattern recognition receptor (PRR) genes, inflammasome-associated genes, and genes involved in downstream inflammatory signaling pathways have emerged as major focuses of research in the field of inflammation genetics. This chapter is organized around the framework of “genetic variation–molecular mechanisms–cellular phenotypes–disease phenotypes–clinical translation” and systematically reviews the major types of inflammation-associated genetic polymorphisms, their molecular mechanisms, and their contributions to the pathogenesis of inflammatory diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, inflammatory bowel disease, and asthma. Furthermore, recent advances in genome-wide association studies (GWAS), fine mapping, expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) and protein quantitative trait locus (pQTL) analyses, single-cell and spatial multi-omics, functional genomics, genome editing, and artificial intelligence are discussed to illustrate how genetic discoveries are being translated into disease risk prediction, molecular stratification, prognostic assessment, pharmacogenomics, and precision therapeutics. It is important to recognize that most complex inflammatory diseases arise from the interplay of multiple genetic factors, environmental exposures, and substantial population heterogeneity. Consequently, genetic associations do not necessarily imply causality, and genetic risk markers identified in research settings should not be interpreted as clinically validated biomarkers that are ready for routine clinical decision-making. With the continued development of multi-omics technologies, single-cell and spatial omics, and artificial intelligence, the field of inflammation genetics is evolving beyond the identification of susceptibility loci toward a deeper understanding of disease mechanisms and the realization of precision medicine.

Enterococcus species are common opportunistic pathogens infecting a wide range of hosts, and often presenting multidrug resistance. Our research has identiﬁed several species of Enterococcus infecting broiler embryos or newly hatched chicks. Genome assemblies for Enterococcus avium and Enterococcus gallinarum isolated from broilers were compared with genomes from poultry and other hosts for phylogenomic relationships and pangenome associations. Three diﬀerent methods demonstrated that host preference in E. gallinarum is associated with genome evolution, with three prominent clusters. In E. avium there is no such evidence for clustering of isolates with respect to host range. The pange-nome analysis identiﬁed a 50- to 51-gene cluster spanning approximately 36 kbp enriched in avian and poultry isolates, relative to human isolates for both species. ChatGPT+ analysis of gene annota-tions from diﬀerent pipelines for this cluster predicted the cluster is likely a new Integrative and Conjugative Element (ICE). Representative ICE inserts were identiﬁed: ICE3 in E. gallinarum EGM181, with ICE1 and ICE2 from our hybrid assembly for E. avium 1788. Boundaries of these ICEs were identiﬁed by alignment to closely related genomes that lacked the ICE. ICE1 and ICE3 are 99% identical, while ICE2 is 94% identical to ICE1/ICE3. Two pipelines were constructed using ChatGPT+ to screen all available genomes from both species, for ICE1-like and ICE2-like, and subsequently extract intact ICEs, including identiﬁcation of ﬂanking genes. E. gallinarum genomes contained 13 ICE1-like and 1 ICE2-like, while E. avium genomes contained 15 ICE1-like and 4 ICE2-like. Only 1788 contained two ICEs. For 31 genomes the ICE insert is downstream of UDP-N-acetylmuramoyl-tripeptide--D-alanyl-D-alanine ligase (murF) and upstream of DEAD-box ATP-dependent RNA helicase (cshA), with all inserts in the same orientation relative to the ﬂanking genes. In 1788 the upstream gene for ICE2 is murF, and downstream gene is glucose uptake protein, while for ICE1 the upstream gene is sapS and downstream gene is cshA. The pipelines identiﬁed an additional 6 E. gallinarum and 5 E. avium genomes with an ICE1 or ICE2 split across two contigs. While 20 of the gene annotations are for hypothetical or poorly deﬁned polypeptides ChatGPT+ ascribes the remainder to Replication Control/Regulatory/Accessory, Conjugative Transfer, Stability/Maintenance, Recombination/Mobil-ity, or Adhesion/Bioﬁlm. Therefore, the role of the ICE in associating bacterial isolates with avian/poultry cannot be determined at this time but likely resides in the 20 hypothetical/poorly deﬁned genes in the adaptation region of these new ICE.

Geographic Information Systems (GIS) have evolved from digital mapping and spatial data management tools into analytical and decision-support environments for contemporary town planning. This review critically synthesizes 20 studies covering GIS applications in urban growth modelling, land-use planning, site suitability, transportation and accessibility, infrastructure planning, environmental management, disaster-risk assessment, development control, public participation, and integration with remote sensing, BIM, artificial intelligence and emerging digital technologies. The reviewed evidence indicates that the principal value of GIS in town planning lies in its ability to integrate heterogeneous spatial and attribute datasets, perform multi-criteria and network-based analysis, represent spatial relationships, visualize alternative development scenarios, and support monitoring and decision-making. However, the literature also shows recurring limitations associated with data quality, temporal updating, interoperability, model calibration and validation, technical capacity, institutional coordination, cost, privacy and unequal access to spatial information. A cross-study synthesis is used to organize GIS applications according to planning function, analytical method, decision stage and technology integration. The review identifies a transition from GIS as a mapping and inventory system toward an integrated planning-support ecosystem combining GIS with remote sensing, BIM, IoT, cloud platforms, 3D visualization and AI/ML. Based on the synthesis, a conceptual GIS-enabled town-planning framework is proposed, linking data acquisition and quality assurance with spatial analysis, scenario modelling, stakeholder participation, decision support and continuous monitoring. The review concludes that future research should prioritize interoperable and continuously updated spatial infrastructures, transparent multi-criteria modelling, validated predictive approaches, human-centred participatory interfaces and integrated GIS–RS–BIM–AI environments.

This study critically examines the ethical frameworks of leading generative AI platforms to understand how they discursively position student writing, construct normative subjects, and redistribute epistemic authority in higher education. By asking what kind of “ethical academic subject” these documents construct and what functions their governance discourses perform, we conducted a critical discourse analysis of publicly available ethical and governance documents from nine widely used AI platforms and one contextual state-regulatory text, using versions retrieved on 1 October 2026. Guided by three research questions, the analysis drew on an integrated framework of posthumanism, sociomateriality, Foucauldian governmentality, and ethics of care, operationalised through Fairclough's three-dimensional model. The analysis reveals how these frameworks discursively construct students as hybrid cognitive agents simultaneously empowered by augmentation and disciplined by algorithmic oversight. We identify six interlocking discursive formations: safety governance, academic integrity regulation, transparency as an epistemic virtue, human-machine augmentation, platform procedural accountability, and relational responsibility, which function not as neutral ethical guides but as a powerful layer of discursively constituted algorithmic governmentality. We argue that platform ethics is discursively positioned to reshape academic authorship and to conduct student behaviour through regimes of corporate and state-aligned governance. The asymmetry between aspirational corporate commitments and directive user obligations is consistent with what the literature terms “ethics-washing”: ethical vocabulary that performs legitimacy while preserving corporate discretion. We identify this as a discursive function, not a demonstrated corporate motive. We also suggest, as a theoretical proposition for future empirical testing, that such regimes may leave limited spaces for tactical student agency. By conceptualising platform policies as claims to educational governing authority, we expose the tensions between empowerment and control embedded in AI-mediated writing and argue for critical platform literacy as an essential response to this parallel governance regime.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Higher education institutions increasingly embrace and regulate Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI). While the cognitive, social, and ethical implications of GenAI are widely discussed in the current scientific discourse, the environmental disruption caused by large-scale GenAI use has remained largely ignored. As GenAI becomes integral to research and education, addressing its environmental impacts has become an increasingly urgent priority. In this Perspective, we argue that mitigating the environmental impact of GenAI requires more than advances in hardware and software efficiency; it also demands a stronger focus on user behavior as a key lever for reducing GenAI’s disruptive environmental impacts. This is particularly important given that every second, millions of prompts are submitted to GenAI systems in support of human learning, research, and knowledge acquisition. Optimizing how users interact with these systems offers scalable behavior-based strategies with the potential to substantially reduce their environmental impacts while requiring relatively modest changes in practice. We present a set of measures to promote the sustainable use of GenAI in higher education and scientific research.

This study investigates the effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a pedagogical tool to address the challenge of engaging secondary students. We explore how an AI music composing application can transform 11th grade Tamil memory poems into musical mnemonics and measure its impact against traditional methods. Grounded in Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning and Gardner's Theory of Multiple Intelligences, This study involved a control group that engaged in traditional reading. The experimental groups listened to the poem set to music: Rendition composed by a human, and three distinct versions (Rap, Carnatic, and Melody) generated by an AI music application. A one-way ANOVA indicated significant differences in memory scores across groups (F(4,207=25.48, p,0.001). AI-generated content performed comparably to human-composed material, with AI-Rap exhibiting the highest effectiveness. These findings confirm the efficacy and scalability of AI audio creation tools in enhancing literature education.

In the modern era we are living in, Artificial Intelligence in Human Resource management made a revolution of how organizations manage employees, identify their talent and helping to manage work Stress and mitigate bias in the hybrid environment. As organizations embrace AI-based tools are transforming the recruitment and performance management and employee relations digital transformation. Nevertheless, the increased pace of using these technologies. poses highly important questions regarding sustainability in the sphere of HRM, especially in respect of balancing technology efficiency with values the human being. This paper examines the process of AI-based digital. change is capable of instilling sustainable HRM activities that boost the welfare of employees, resilience, and work ecosystems in the hybrid work environment.

Systematic reviews show that patients generally support AI in gastroenterology for tasks such as image analysis, with a strong emphasis on the need for clinician oversight and addressing concerns about privacy and reliability.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Coastal fishing communities depend on marine resources yet face significant occupational and environmental health risks. This study asssessed health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and self-reported accidents and health outcomes among adults in three coastal municipalities of Palawan, Philippines. A cross-sectional survey recruited 431 adults across 10 barangays, with 401 complete responses analyzed. The HRQoL was assessed using the Philippine Short Form-12 (SF-12), producing Physical Component Summary (PCS-12) and Mental Component Summary (MCS-12) scores. Fifteen self-reported health items were examined using exploratory factor analysis, identifying three domains: marine accidents, musculoskeletal complaints, and infections and skin diseases. Women had higher odds of reporting marine-related accidents compared thaan men (OR = 2.07; 95% CI: 1.87–2.54). More than half of respondents (56.9%, n = 228) had PCS-12 ≤50 (mean 48.3 ± 5.7), indicating poor physical health, while 26.4% (n = 106) scored MCS-12 ≤42 (mean 47.3 ± 8.3), suggesting possible mental health concerns. Musculoskeletal complaints were the most prevalent health outcome, affecting up to 71.1% of respondents, while those in the poorest marine-based income bracket had nearly twice the odds of reporting infections and skin diseases (OR = 1.87; 95% CI: 1.22–3.86). The HRQoL varied by study site, gender, age, and education, whereas ethnicity, religion, and coastal proximity were not significantly associated. These findings showed that women and low-income fishers face greater occupational and environmental health risks. Interventions should prioritize gender-responsive safety, ergonomic support, accessible healthcare, and stronger social protection. Further qualitative research is needed to clarify the pathways that drive these disparities.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) reach users worldwide, personal counseling has emerged as one of their most consequential applications, sometimes in life-critical situations. Yet broader access does not mean equal support. The text these models learn from disproportionately reflects people with the freedom to act, embedding an implicit assumption that users can leave, report, seek help, or appeal. Existing benchmarks largely inherit this assumption, overlooking users whose agency is constrained by structural conditions such as war, statelessness, and displacement. Meanwhile, models are increasingly shaped by normative frameworks such as Constitutional AI, often grounded in ideals like human rights, even as many users live where those rights offer little protection or recourse. We introduce HEARSAYBENCH, a human-authored dataset of 400 test cases with in-region human verification grounded in scenarios where structural barriers stand between a person and the exercise of their rights. Built from United Nations and other human rights reports, the scenarios span over 80 regions and cover social, environmental, and personal constraints. Drawing on Nobel laureate Amartya Sen's Capabilities Approach, HEARSAYBENCH tests whether models can distinguish what a person is formally entitled to do from what they are actually able to do. Across 14 proprietary and open-weight models, every model infers a user's situation more accurately than it advises on it. Stronger models narrow this gap, but their recommendations remain unsafe to follow. Models may understand lives shaped by constraint, yet that knowledge remains hearsay if it cannot translate into advice people can act on. Those people are not alignment's long tail; they are among the users for whom good guidance matters most. HEARSAYBENCH makes this failure measurable, a step toward systems that serve the world as it is rather than as assumed.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The objective of this research paper is to study how game-theoretical models help in determining the optimal decision in a mid-game situation where there is uncertainty, high complexity related to strategies, and a large number of options available for making a decision. The paper discusses the basic ideas such as normal form and extensive form games, Nash equilibrium, subgame perfect equilibrium, Bayesian games, stochastic games, and mixed strategies that one should use when making decisions when there is insufficient information available. Specifically, the paper analyzes the methods of Bayesian belief updating, stochastic state transitions, heuristic search, Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) method, and reinforcement learning, the idea of which is to allow the identification of best decisions in cases when the computation of equilibrium is very difficult. The authors examine the examples referring to different games such as chess, poker, go, and real-time strategy games and show how game-theoretical concepts can be combined with computational solutions. The discussion brings up a significant number of drawbacks such as computational complexity, lack of full information, bounded rationality, incorrect models, and dependence on data quality. In this paper, the authors conclude that the integration of game theory with simulation and artificial intelligence provides a practical framework for developing robust and near-optimal strategies in complex uncertain environments.

Background Teachers and learners now use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in inquiry-based learning (IBL), but we know little about which inquiry phases GenAI supports, who uses it and what outcomes studies report across disciplines. Methods Following PRISMA 2020, we searched Scopus on 6 October 2026 for empirical journal articles published in English from 2022 to 2026. Of 267 records screened, we sought 110 reports, assessed 89 in full text and included 66 studies. We coded the studies with a 29-variable codebook and mapped GenAI use onto the five inquiry phases (orientation, conceptualization, investigation, conclusion and discussion). We synthesized the findings descriptively and did not appraise study quality. Results Most studies appeared in 2025–2026 and took place in higher or teacher education; more than half came from fields outside science. Studies used ChatGPT or other OpenAI GPT models in 71.2% of cases, mostly as unmodified chatbots, and GenAI served most often as an information source (60.6%). Studies reported GenAI support most often in the investigation phase (68.2%) and least often in orientation (30.3%); 11 studies covered all five phases, and for most phases about half of the studies did not say whether GenAI was used. Half of the studies reported positive outcomes. Thirteen of the 14 comparisons with instruction without AI were positive, whereas comparisons between GenAI designs split evenly between positive and mixed results. Inaccuracy (31.8%) and over-reliance (24.2%) were the challenges studies reported most often. Conclusions GenAI mainly supplies information during investigation and seldom supports the full inquiry cycle. Some comparative evidence favors GenAI designs that withhold direct answers or add metacognitive scaffolds, but this evidence is thin. Future studies should report the phases GenAI supports, measure inquiry skills directly and compare GenAI designs with one another.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the level of agreement between ChatGPT-5.5 and human assessments when appraising the methodological quality and overall confidence of the results of systematic reviews (SRs) with meta-analysis (MA) in endodontology. METHODS: SRs with MA related to endodontology and published in English between 2021 and 2024 were included. The methodological quality of the SRs was appraised by three human experts using AMSTAR 2, and a consensus dataset was generated. ChatGPT-5.5 was applied to generate AMSTAR 2 item-level ratings and overall confidence classifications for each SR through three newly created accounts. Agreement between consolidated ChatGPT-5.5 ratings and human consensus was assessed for both overall confidence and each AMSTAR 2 item. Overall-confidence agreement was evaluated under the primary criterion (Partial Yes = Yes) and an alternative sensitivity criterion (Partial Yes = No). Direct agreement and linearly weighted Cohen's kappa were calculated, and complete 3/3 agreement was used to assess consistency across ChatGPT-5.5 accounts. RESULTS: One hundred SRs were included. Human consensus and ChatGPT-5.5 classified 47 and 85 SRs, respectively, as critically low. Under the primary criterion (Partial Yes = Yes), overall confidence matched in 52/100 SRs (52%; weighted κ = 0.182). Under the alternative criterion (Partial Yes = No), agreement increased to 83%, while weighted κ remained similar (κ = 0.173), indicating that direct agreement was sensitive to the handling of Partial Yes. Item-level agreement varied substantially. Overall confidence was identical across the three ChatGPT-5.5 accounts in 85 SRs, and global item-level 3/3 agreement was 86.12%. In the 100 sampled SRs, 15% met the criterion for reporting primary-study funding and 21% for justifying study designs. CONCLUSION: Overall-confidence direct agreement was sensitive to the handling of Partial Yes ratings, whereas chance-corrected agreement remained similar under both criteria. ChatGPT-5.5 assigned lower overall confidence classifications more frequently than human consensus, and agreement varied across AMSTAR 2 domains. Although outputs were frequently consistent across the three ChatGPT-5.5 accounts, between-account consistency did not ensure concordance with human judgements. The findings do not support the use of ChatGPT-5.5 as an independent AMSTAR 2 assessor; any exploratory application requires item-by-item verification by reviewers with methodological expertise.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Psychological screening is easily displaced by physiological safety checks when preoperative teams have little time and too few staff. Healthcare systems are already affected by widespread workforce shortages and clinician burnout. We suggest that preoperative anxiety consequently often remains unmanaged, with implications for postoperative recovery and hospital workload. Generic educational materials do not adequately address differences in patients’ anxiety, and “health data poverty” can further exclude vulnerable groups. We propose a conceptual human-machine collaborative (HMC) generative artificial intelligence framework to address these clinical and occupational problems together. In the proposed doctor–patient–AI feedback loop, natural language processing would dynamically assess psychosocial risk and guide patient-specific, multimodal education, including dialect-adapted voice agents, as a source of baseline emotional support. Routine interactions would be automated under clinician supervision. Our hypothesis is that this arrangement may conserve clinicians’ limited emotional bandwidth and allow healthier “cognitive reappraisal” in place of chronic fatigue. Implementation science provides a basis for considering how lightweight AI models could be scaled across regional health networks to bring standardized psychoeducation to under-resourced rural areas. This remains a theoretical pathway. Through sociotechnical governance and “data solidarity” to fairly manage algorithmic liability, the framework is still a conceptual framework, but it is operational: it proposes a path to improve perioperative workflows and health equity in the face of severe human resource constraints.

documents.abstract: This chapter proposes the Human-Centered Cognitive Architecture for Research Environments (HCCARE), a conceptual framework for embedding explainable artificial intelligence within research data infrastructure. Current cognitive data systems trade researcher-facing transparency for operational performance, creating conditions for miscalibrated trust in AI-assisted research. HCCARE specifies four integrated layers connected by provenance chains: a transparent data layer, cognitive reasoning layer, adaptive explanation layer, and participatory governance layer. Three design principles govern the architecture: interpretability by design, participatory data governance, and adaptive explanation generation. A synthesis of literature on XAI, intelligent information systems, and human-centered design grounds the framework. Empirical validation against benchmark datasets constitutes the immediate next step.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly explored for medical image interpretation, yet their capability for tooth-level abnormality detection on dental panoramic radiographs (OPG) remains largely unquantified. Moreover, reference-standard construction for such evaluations usually lacks a transparent human-in-the-loop review pipeline. We developed an interactive web-based review platform with multi-view visualization (original and annotated images), finding-by-finding auditing, and FDI tooth-number recommendation with accept/reject/manual confirmation, from which an expert-reviewed OPG reference standard of 233 cases, admitted by consensus verification of two senior oral clinicians (1,859 tooth–finding pairs across 1,600 annotated tooth positions; FDI tooth numbers and a closed 20-class disease vocabulary), was derived. On this reference standard, we compared four MLLMs — doubao_web, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, Gemini-3.6-flash-medium and M365 Copilot (GPT 5.6) — on two tasks: tooth-level finding presence and tooth–finding association (classification). The four models were accessed through two arms, an API arm and a consumer web arm, which were not run under matched conditions; within-arm contrasts are the primary inference and cross-arm contrasts are descriptive. Precision, recall and F1 were computed with case-level bootstrap 95% confidence intervals; paired binary outcomes were tested with exact McNemar tests, re-estimated under case-level cluster-robust variance with Holm correction; per-case F1 with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests; and inter-model error independence with Cohen’s kappa. The 233-case evaluation set was drawn from a corpus compiled from an openly licensed public collection together with radiographs acquired at the Department of Stomatology, Yijishan Hospital of Wannan Medical College, with all patient-identifiable information removed before analysis; the study was approved by the institutional ethics committee. M365 Copilot GPT 5.6 showed the highest point estimates on both tasks (tooth F1 = 0.642, pair F1 = 0.485), followed by Gemini-3.6-flash-medium (0.610/0.456). Within the web arm, M365 significantly outperformed doubao_web (0.501/0.348; both \(p < 0.001\) ); within the API arm, Gemini significantly outperformed Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct (0.537/0.340; both \(p < 0.001\) ). The cross-arm gap between M365 and Gemini was borderline in per-case tooth F1 ( p = 0.052) and remained significant in the tooth-level McNemar test under case-level cluster-robust variance ( p = 0.005; Holm-adjusted p = 0.010). The two strongest models were positively correlated ( \(\kappa\) = 0.316), while all other pairwise model \(\kappa\) values were negative ( \(-0.203\) to \(-0.007\) ), indicating largely independent error patterns. All models performed poorly on caries and periapical lesions (pair F1 < 0.1). Current MLLMs performed relatively better on high-contrast structures (e.g., impacted teeth, F1 = 0.831 for M365, 0.814 for Gemini-3.6) but remained inadequate for subtle lesions; the errors of the four models were largely independent rather than complementary, and a two-model cross-check improved tooth-level union recall from 0.668 to 0.727–0.854 at the cost of arbitrating 20.4–42.3% of positive teeth (a descriptive cross-model quantification, given the unmatched access arms), which supports a two-model cross-check plus human review workflow when that arbitration cost is acceptable. The proposed review platform provides a reproducible, audit-trail reference-standard construction pipeline for benchmarking MLLMs in dental imaging.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Institutional responses to Generative AI (GenAI) in higher education, from outright prohibition to open permission, leave students without the necessary conditions to engage with GenAI critically. In language teacher education, where assessment should support students in consolidating a professional identity, the lack of a principled approach to GenAI is problematic. This article proposes the redesign of two linked assessments in a final-year undergraduate module on Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages (TESOL), arguing that humanising GenAI use in TESOL assessment offers a way forward that places learner agency, well-being and professional identity at the centre of assessment design. Redesigned briefs are made openly available as supplementary materials, inviting implementation, evaluation and adaptation across contexts.

The paper explores the transformative potential of synergistic integration between Generative AI (GenAI) and Digital Humans in the context of natural disaster management. Traditional crisis notification systems often fail due to structural inelasticity and inability to overcome cognitive tunneling and panic in the threatened population. The paper proposes a new conceptual framework - “Cognitive-Affective Crisis Synergy” - in which GenAI functions as the operational computational core (the brain) and Digital Humans serve as an empathetic, multimodal interface (the face). This is a conceptual and theoretical contribution; the framework is illustrated through practical scenarios rather than empirical validation. Practical scenarios are analyzed across the three phases of crisis management: experiential learning (prevention), scalable tactical dissemination with embedded autonomous sign language translation (response), and virtual psychological triage (recovery). Special attention is paid to ethical and technological challenges, including algorithmic hallucinations, the Uncanny Valley effect under stress, legal liability assignment, and the protection of user biometric sovereignty. The paper concludes with practical recommendations for implementing RAG architectures and Edge AI systems to build a sustainable, inclusive, and humanized technological infrastructure for population protection.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Wind turbine systems are frequently subjected to complex operational conditions, leading to frequent quality issues that trigger warnings and alarms, and this demands rapid and accurate quality check with Root Cause Analysis (RCA). Conventional RCA processes rely fully on manual inspection and expert interpretation that involves human, resulting in significant time delays, increased operational costs, and high turbine downtime. To address these challenges, this paper presents a Hybrid AI Agent Framework that integrates Machine Vision and Multi Modal Data Fusion for automated preliminary RCA in wind turbine alarm systems. The proposed system consists of YOLO based machine vision for physical defect detection, advanced thermal image analysis for temperature anomaly identification, and historical SCADA data integration to generate a comprehensive diagnostic context. A novel AI agent-based RCA engine is developed, which synthesizes multi source inputs and produces structured root cause insights using a DMAIC (Define-Measure-Analyse-Improve-Control) framework and that also includes Fishbone and 5-Why quality analytical methodologies from six sigma quality principle. The architecture is implemented using a scalable Fast API based backend, integrated with a user-friendly web interface that has turbine data retrieval, and real time analysis. The system supports both single instance and batch processing, enabling efficient handling of large datasets. Automated alerting mechanisms are incorporated through email notifications, ensuring timely communication of detected anomalies and quality issues. Validation of the system is carried out using synthetic and open-source datasets, demonstrating its capability to accurately identify defects, detect thermal hotspots, and generate meaningful preliminary RCA reports. The proposed framework significantly reduces dependency on manual inspection, minimizes turbine downtime, reduces loss production factor (LPF) and enhances operational efficiency. Overall, the system establishes a scalable and intelligent foundation for future development of fully autonomous wind turbine diagnostics and predictive maintenance solutions.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: Preoperative prediction of intracranial meningioma consistency may improve surgical planning by anticipating the ease of internal debulking, operative difficulty, and the feasibility of minimally invasive approaches. Numerous imaging biomarkers have been proposed, ranging from routine MRI measurements to advanced quantitative techniques and artificial intelligence-based models. This scoping review aimed to critically evaluate their diagnostic performance, methodological quality, biological rationale, and potential for clinical implementation. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched from database inception to July 2026 in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Original human studies assessing MRI-derived biomarkers for the preoperative prediction of meningioma consistency were eligible. Studies were grouped into routine MRI, advanced MRI, and artificial intelligence-based approaches. Methodological quality was assessed using QUADAS-2, the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale, and the Radiomics Quality Score, as appropriate. Owing to substantial methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively. Thirty-five publications were included: 14 evaluated routine MRI biomarkers, 13 advanced MRI techniques, and 8 radiomics or artificial intelligence approaches. Among routine sequences, T2-weighted signal intensity ratios, particularly the tumor-to-cerebellar peduncle T2-weighted intensity ratio, showed the most consistent association with softer tumors and was the most readily deployable in routine practice. Diffusion-derived parameters provided complementary but less reproducible information. Magnetic resonance elastography demonstrated the strongest evidence among advanced techniques by directly quantifying tissue stiffness and correlating with intraoperative consistency and histopathological features. Radiomics and deep-learning models reported high apparent predictive performance, frequently with AUCs above 0.90, but most studies were retrospective, single-center, internally validated, and in some cases based on overlapping patient cohorts. Routine T2-based biomarkers currently offer the best balance between accessibility and predictive value. Magnetic resonance elastography provides greater biomechanical specificity, whereas artificial intelligence approaches remain promising but insufficiently validated for routine use. Standardized reference standards, multicenter external validation, and stronger biological correlation are required before widespread clinical implementation.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Limited access to qualified instructors and opportunities for guided practice remains a barrier for many people learning American Sign Language (ASL), including hearing learners and newly signing Deaf people. Interactive technologies that provide real-time, accessible feedback may help lower these barriers and support wider adoption of ASL. We developed ASL Champ!, a standalone virtual reality (VR) application that supports introductory ASL vocabulary learning in immersive environments. ASL Champ! provides automated feedback via a deep learning–based sign recognition algorithm using the VR headset's built-in cameras. We evaluated ASL Champ! in a within-participant experimental study comparing it with a conventional 2D video-based learning platform (Edpuzzle), focusing on user experience, cognitive workload, and behavioral outcomes relevant to accessible learning systems. Adult non-signers ( n = 11) completed matched ASL lessons using ASL Champ! (VR) and Edpuzzle (2D) and completed assessments of receptive ASL comprehension and expressive sign production. Results showed that VR-based learning imposed a higher cognitive workload than the 2D platform, while receptive comprehension was near ceiling across conditions. In contrast, signs learned in VR were produced more accurately, particularly with respect to handshape. Despite the higher workload, most participants preferred the VR platform for continued learning. These findings characterize key design trade-offs in accessible sign language learning technologies and inform the development of future immersive systems for ASL learning.

This article investigates the creative potential and practical use of artificial intelligence in architectural visualization by testing three free platforms: Fabrie, Mnml AI and LookX AI Cloud, on a real project involving the design of a single-story house with a summer kitchen. The study aims to assess the extent to which these AI tools can support or enhance the development and refinement of architectural visualizations, both through the generation of new renders based on conceptual sketches and through the processing of existing visual data. The methodology involves the comparative analysis of the platforms’ outputs using four evaluation criteria: clarity of spatial perception, level of detailing, emotional expressiveness, and the format and quality of the final exported visual data. Based on this framework, the study identifies the respective strengths and limitations of each AI system, highlighting distinctive characteristics in render quality, user interface, and interpretive responsiveness to design prompts. The article also formulates practical guidelines for data preparation and prompt formulation, addressing technical constraints, model sensitivity, and the iterative nature of human-AI interaction. A key contribution of the study lies in its dual methodological approach: rendering experiments were conducted in two modes: generation from a blank sketch and enhancement of an existing render, thereby illuminating how AI tools can be integrated into different phases of the design workflow. The study also reflects on the broader implications of human-AI collaboration in architectural practice, focusing on how authorship, visual language, and creative decision-making are redefined in the context of automated design assistance. The scientific novelty of this research lies in its detailed, real-case-based evaluation of emerging AI visualization platforms in architectural work. Its practical significance is evident in the set of recommendations it provides to architects, designers, and educators exploring AI as a co-creative design partner.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is widely used by social media platforms to personalize feeds, recommend videos, suggest accounts, and select advertisements.However, users may not understand why a particular item appears or how their data influences these recommendations.Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) aims to make AI outputs more understandable to people.This paper presents a survey-based research framework for examining the relationship between perceived explanation clarity and usefulness, user trust, privacy perception, and willingness to engage with recommended content.A questionnaire with demographic questions and five-point response scales is proposed.To demonstrate the planned analysis, a simulated dataset of 150 records is used for descriptive illustration.In this simulated dataset, mean ratings were 3.43 for explanation clarity, 3.54 for explanation usefulness, 3.19 for trust, 3.50 for privacy confidence, and 3.30 for engagement willingness on a five-point scale.These figures are illustrative only and do not represent real participants or establish real-world relationships.The paper outlines a methodology for collecting genuine responses and analysing them using descriptive statistics, reliability checks, correlation, and regression where appropriate.The work highlights the need to consider both transparency and privacy when designing user-centred AI recommendations.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
